claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 2. STRATEGY TO ENFORCE PROHIBITION ON IMPORTATION OF GOODS MADE THROUGH FORCED LABOR IN THE XINJIANG UYGHUR AUTONOMOUS REGION. (a) Public Comment.-- (1) <<NOTE: Deadline. Federal Register, publication. Notice.>> In general.--Not later than 30 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force, established under section 741 of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement Implementation Act (19 U.S.C. 4681), shall publish in the Federal Register a notice soliciting public comments on how best to ensure that goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor in the People's Republic of China, including by Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tibetans, and members of other persecuted groups in the People's Republic of China, and especially in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, are not imported into the United States. (2) Period for comment.--The Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force shall provide the public with not less than 45 days to submit comments in response to the notice required by paragraph (1). (b) Public Hearing.-- (1) <<NOTE: Deadline.>> In general.--Not later than 45 days after the close of the period to submit comments under subsection (a)(2), the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force shall conduct a public hearing inviting witnesses to testify with respect to the use of forced labor in the People's Republic of China and potential measures, including the measures described in paragraph (2), to prevent the importation of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor in the People's Republic of China into the United States. (2) Measures described.--The measures described in this paragraph are-- (A) measures that can be taken to trace the origin of goods, offer greater supply chain transparency, and identify third country supply chain routes for goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor in the People's Republic of China; and (B) other measures for ensuring that goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor do not enter the United States. (c) <<NOTE: Consultation.>> Development of Strategy.--After receiving public comments under subsection (a) and holding the hearing required by subsection (b), the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force, in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence, shall develop a strategy for supporting enforcement of Section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307) to prevent the importation into the United States of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor in the People's Republic of China. (d) Elements.--The strategy developed under subsection (c) shall include the following: (1) <<NOTE: Assessment.>> A comprehensive assessment of the risk of importing goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part [[Page 135 STAT. 1527]] with forced labor in the People's Republic of China, including from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region or made by Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tibetans, or members of other persecuted groups in any other part of the People's Republic of China, that identifies, to the extent feasible-- (A) threats, including through the potential involvement in supply chains of entities that may use forced labor, that could lead to the importation into the United States from the People's Republic of China, including through third countries, of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor; and (B) what procedures can be implemented or improved to reduce such threats. (2) <<NOTE: Evaluation.>> A comprehensive description and evaluation-- (A) of ``pairing assistance'' and ``poverty alleviation'' or any other government labor scheme that includes the forced labor of Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tibetans, or members of other persecuted groups outside of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region or similar programs of the People's Republic of China in which work or services are extracted from Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tibetans, or members of other persecuted groups through the threat of penalty or for which the Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tibetans, or members of other persecuted groups have not offered themselves voluntarily; and (B) <<NOTE: Lists.>> that includes-- (i) a list of entities in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region that mine, produce, or manufacture wholly or in part any goods, wares, articles and merchandise with forced labor; (ii) a list of entities working with the government of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor or receive forced labor or Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, or members of other persecuted groups out of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region; (iii) a list of products mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part by entities on the list required by clause (i) or (ii); (iv) a list of entities that exported products described in clause (iii) from the People's Republic of China into the United States; (v) a list of facilities and entities, including the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps, that source material from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region or from persons working with the government of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region or the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps for purposes of the ``poverty alleviation'' program or the ``pairing- assistance'' program or any other government labor scheme that uses forced labor; (vi) <<NOTE: Plan.>> a plan for identifying additional facilities and entities described in clause (v); (vii) <<NOTE: Plan.>> an enforcement plan for each such entity whose goods, wares articles, or merchandise are exported into the United States, which may include [[Page 135 STAT. 1528]] issuing withhold release orders to support enforcement of section 4 with respect to the entity; (viii) a list of high-priority sectors for enforcement, which shall include cotton, tomatoes, and polysilicon; and (ix) <<NOTE: Plan.>> an enforcement plan for each such high-priority sector. (3) <<NOTE: Recommenda- tions.>> Recommendations for efforts, initiatives, and tools and technologies to be adopted to ensure that U.S. Customs and Border Protection can accurately identify and trace goods made in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region entering at any of the ports of the United States. (4) <<NOTE: Examination.>> A description of how U.S. Customs and Border Protection plans to enhance its use of legal authorities and other tools to ensure that no goods are entered at any of the ports of the United States in violation of section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307), including through the initiation of pilot programs to test the viability of technologies to assist in the examination of such goods. (5) A description of the additional resources necessary for U.S. Customs and Border Protection to ensure that no goods are entered at any of the ports of the United States in violation of section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307). (6) Guidance to importers with respect to-- (A) due diligence, effective supply chain tracing, and supply chain management measures to ensure that such importers do not import any goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor from the People's Republic of China, especially from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region; (B) the type, nature, and extent of evidence that demonstrates that goods originating in the People's Republic of China were not mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region; and (C) the type, nature, and extent of evidence that demonstrates that goods originating in the People's Republic of China, including goods detained or seized pursuant to section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307), were not mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor. (7) <<NOTE: Plan. Update.>> A plan to coordinate and collaborate with appropriate nongovernmental organizations and private sector entities to implement and update the strategy developed under subsection (c). (e) Submission of Strategy.-- (1) <<NOTE: Consultation. Reports.>> In general.--Not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, and annually thereafter, the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force, in consultation with the Department of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence, shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report that-- (A) in the case of the first such report, sets forth the strategy developed under subsection (c); and (B) in the case of any subsequent such report, sets forth any updates to the strategy. [[Page 135 STAT. 1529]] (2) <<NOTE: Deadline.>> Updates of certain matters.--Not less frequently than annually after the submission under paragraph (1)(A) of the strategy developed under subsection (c), the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees updates to the strategy with respect to the matters described in clauses (i) through (ix) of subsection (d)(2)(B). (3) Form of report.--Each report required by paragraph (1) shall be submitted in unclassified form, but may include a classified annex, if necessary. (4) Public availability.--The unclassified portion of each report required by paragraph (1) shall be made available to the public. (f) Rule of Construction.--Nothing in this section may be construed to limit the application of regulations in effect on or measures taken before the date of the enactment of this Act to prevent the importation of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor into the United States, including withhold release orders issued before such date of enactment.

claim_source_map.passage: Public Reporting of Chinese Military Companies Operating in the United States Pub. L. 116–283, div. A, title XII, §1260H, Jan. 1, 2021, 134 Stat. 3965, as amended by Pub. L. 118–159, div. A, title XIII, §1346, Dec. 23, 2024, 138 Stat. 2123, provided that: "(a) Determination .—The Secretary of Defense shall identify each entity the Secretary determines, based on the most recent information available, is operating directly or indirectly in the United States or any of its territories and possessions, that is a Chinese military company. "(b) Reporting and Publication.— "(1) Annual report .—Not later than April 15, 2021, and annually thereafter until December 31, 2030, the Secretary shall submit to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives a list of each entity identified pursuant to subsection (a) to be a Chinese military company, in classified and unclassified forms, and shall include in such submission, as applicable, a justification for adding any entities to the list and for deleting any entities from a prior list. "(2) Concurrent publication.— "(A) In general .—Concurrent with the submission of each list described in paragraph (1), the Secretary shall publish the unclassified portion of such list in the Federal Register. "(B) Inclusion .—The publication required by subparagraph (A) shall include, for each entity included in the unclassified portion of such list, the justification for inclusion in such list. "(3) Annual revisions .—The Secretary shall make additions or deletions to the most recent list submitted under paragraph (1) not less frequently than annually based on the latest information available. "(4) Language requirement .—The Secretary shall prepare the list required by paragraph (1) in English and in Mandarin Chinese. If the name of a Chinese military company included on the list is referred to by the Government of China in a language other than English or Mandarin Chinese, the Secretary shall also include on the list the name of that company in that language. "(c) Consultation .—The Secretary may consult with the head of any appropriate Federal department or agency in making the determinations described in subsection (a) and shall transmit a copy of each list submitted under subsection (b)(1) to the heads of each appropriate Federal department and agency. "(d) Defense Industrial Base Report.— "(1) In general .—Not later than December 31, 2026, and biennially thereafter through December 31, 2031, the Secretary shall submit to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives a report on the status of Department of Defense procurement restrictions on entities included in the list described in subsection (b)(1). "(2) Elements .—Each report required by paragraph (1) shall include the following: "(A) A list of each entity included in the list described in subsection (b)(1) that is likely present in the United States defense industrial base. "(B) Available unclassified data on any such entity and its presence within the United States defense industrial base. "(C) A description of any update to policies or procedures implemented to enforce procurement restrictions on entities included in the list described in subsection (b)(1). "(e) Procedures for Implementation .—The Secretary of Defense shall establish such reasonable procedures as are necessary to implement the provisions of this section, including for obtaining information from outside entities relevant to the list described in subsection (b)(1) and procedures for removal of entities from the list described in subsection (b)(1). "(f) Judicial Review .— In any judicial review of a determination made under this section, if the determination was based on classified information (as defined in section 1(a) of the Classified Information Procedures Act [18 U.S.C. App.]) such information may be submitted to the reviewing court ex parte and in camera. This subsection does not confer or imply any right to judicial review. "(g) Definitions .—In this section: "(1) Affiliated with .—The term 'affiliated with' means in close formal or informal association. "(2) Chinese military company .—The term 'Chinese military company'— "(A) does not include natural persons; "(B) means an entity that is— "(i)(I) directly or indirectly owned by, controlled by, or beneficially owned by, affiliated with, or in an official or unofficial capacity acting as an agent of or on behalf of, the People's Liberation Army, Chinese military and paramilitary elements, security forces, police, law enforcement, border control, the People's Armed Police, the Ministry of State Security (MSS), or any other organization subordinate to the Central Military Commission of the Chinese Communist Party, the Chinese Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council (SASAC), or the State Administration of Science, Technology, and Industry for National Defense (SASTIND); or "(II) identified as a military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base; and "(ii) engaged in providing commercial services, manufacturing, producing, or exporting; and "(C) includes a wholly-owned or wholly-controlled subsidiary or wholly-owned or wholly-controlled affiliate of such an entity or any entity that owns in the aggregate, directly or indirectly, 50 percent or more of any entity or entities described in subparagraph (B). "(3) Military-civil fusion contributor .—The term 'military-civil fusion contributor' includes any of the following: "(A) Entities knowingly receiving assistance from the Government of China or the Chinese Communist Party through science, technology, research, and industrial efforts initiated, granted, or created by, or provided under, or related to, the Chinese military industrial planning apparatus, or in furtherance of Chinese military industrial planning objectives, including selection or designation as a 'Single Champion', 'Little Giant', or any other successor selection or designation as an enterprise associated with industrial planning or military-civil fusion efforts. "(B) Entities managed, overseen, or supervised by, otherwise under the control of, or affiliated with (including by means of formal participation in research partnerships and projects)— "(i) the Chinese Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT); "(ii) the State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council (SASAC); "(iii) the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense (SASTIND); "(iv) the Ministry of State Security (MSS); or "(v) the People's Liberation Army. "(C) Entities receiving assistance, operational direction or policy guidance from the State Administration for Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense. "(D) Any entities or subsidiaries defined as a 'defense enterprise' by the State Council of the People's Republic of China. "(E) Entities residing in or affiliated with a military-civil fusion enterprise zone or receiving assistance from the Government of China through such enterprise zone. "(F) Entities awarded with receipt of military production licenses by the Government of China, including a Weapons and Equipment Research and Production Unit Classified Qualification Permit, Weapons and Equipment Research and Production Certificate, Weapons and Equipment Quality Management System Certificate, or Equipment Manufacturing Unit Qualification. "(G) Entities that advertise on national, provincial, and non-governmental military equipment procurement platforms in the People's Republic of China. "(H) Any other entities the Secretary determines is appropriate. "(4) Operating directly or indirectly in the united states or any of its territories and possessions .—With respect to an entity, the term 'operating directly or indirectly in the United States or any of its territories and possessions' includes an entity selling goods in, or receiving goods or services from, the United States or any of its territories or possessions, regardless of whether the entity has a physical presence in the United States. "(5) People's liberation army .—The term 'People's Liberation Army' means the land, naval, and air military services, the People's Armed Police, the Strategic Support Force, the Rocket Force, and any other related security or intelligence element within the Government of China or the Chinese Communist Party that the Secretary determines is appropriate, including other Chinese military and paramilitary elements, security forces, police, law enforcement, border control, and the Ministry of State Security."

action_observations.compact: Foushee opposed concurrence in that complete Senate replacement; no preferred alternative or separate component position is established. Selected Senate H.R. 1 provisions would fund border infrastructure and detention, set fiscal 2025 asylum filing/pending fee floors of $100 each and specified asylum/parole/TPS employment-authorization initial/renewal fee floors of $550/$275, with distinct duration and termination rules. This is a whole-replacement concurrence choice, with qualifications.
detail: Foushee opposed concurrence in that complete Senate replacement; no preferred alternative or separate component position is established.

This July3 House concurrence concerns the Senate's July1 EAS, which strikes all after the first word and replaces the earlier H.R.1 text. It is the complete multi-domain reconciliation replacement, not a second passage of the unchanged House bill or a separate vote on its Immigration components. Selected Immigration highlights here concern border infrastructure, detention and asylum fees; other immigration-related benefits, taxes, employment authorization, child-sponsor, reimbursement and enforcement provisions are not exhaustively described. Section90001 would appropriate an additional $46.55billion for fiscal2025 to CBP, available until September30,2029, for new/replacement primary, waterborne and secondary barriers, access roads, detection attributes and ground preparation for CBP operations and barrier construction/maintenance. The different House60001 accounts are not silently used to define this replacement amount or its purposes. Section90003 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. Aliens MAY be detained at family centers pending an INA removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Single-adult detention standards are set in the Secretary's discretion CONSISTENT WITH APPLICABLE LAW. The family-center definition covers apprehended/encountered family units, including children who are not statutorily defined unaccompanied alien children, and does not reproduce the House's express regardless-of-State-licensing clause.6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, under18 age, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody. Neither the capacity funding nor permission establishes automatic detention/removal of every alien, elimination of all legal constraints or actual operations. Section100002 requires an additional fee upon filing an asylum application. The fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or the amount set by DHS/the Attorney General, as applicable, by rule; it cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 the prior fiscal-year fee is increased by the printed July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; uncredited receipts go to Treasury. This $100 filing floor differs from the House's $1,000 floor. Section100009 separately requires an additional fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an asylum application remains pending. Its fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or a DHS rule amount, followed by the printed CPI-U annual adjustment with the increment rounded DOWN TO THE NEAREST DOLLAR; receipts go to Treasury and the fee cannot be waived/reduced. Do not transfer that rounding to the initial-filing fee or back to the House's differently printed yearly formula. Section100018 changes pre-vote INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL and replaces the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language with preserved additional adjudication/naturalization-fee authority under286(m). The baseline already authorized asylum-consideration, employment-authorization and asylum-based adjustment fees;1356(m)/(n) govern existing account/cost-recovery context. No first-ever fee authority, new asylum eligibility test from that edit, specific implemented collection rule or actual payment is inferred. Employment-authorization fees are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. Senate100003 requires additional initial application fees for asylum applicants under1158(d)(2), paroled aliens andTPS employment-authorization applicants under1254a(a)(1)(B). Each fiscal2025 floor is$550 or a higher DHS rule amount, with no waiver/reduction and fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. The asylum-initial subsection contains no House-style six-month duration sentence; it credits25percent of fees collected PURSUANT TO THIS SUBSECTION to USCIS's existing fee account, retained/expended without further appropriation with NOT LESS THAN50percent of the credited share for benefit-fraud detection/prevention, and sends the rest to Treasury. Parole/TPS initial fees go to Treasury; their initial authorizations last one year or the duration of parole/TPS respectively, whichever is shorter. Senate100010 and100012 set separate parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal/extension fiscal2025 fee floors of$275, possible higher DHS rule amounts and later CPI increments rounded down to$10. Each sends25percent to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation and the rest to Treasury; no waiver/reduction.100012 states one year or the duration of the designation ofTPS, whichever is shorter.100010 literally says employment authorization for each paroled alien, OR ANY RENEWAL OR EXTENSION OF SUCH PAROLE, shall be valid for one year or parole duration, whichever is shorter. Preserve this printed antecedent and leave its application unresolved; do not rewrite it into a new parole-eligibility rule or import House six-month text. Senate100011 imposes at least$275 for each asylum-based employment-authorization renewal/extension, with25percent credited to USCIS's existing fee account without further appropriation, the rest to Treasury and no waiver/reduction. It prints no annual CPI formula or House-style six-month limit. It retains the three termination points: immediately after asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. It does not reproduce the separate House70013(d) prohibition on later grants/renewals/extensions absent a FederalCourtOfAppeals remand. Absence of that House sentence does not establish unlimited permission or erase other law. The complete pre-vote1158(d)(2) already permits regulated asylum-based work authorization while denying entitlement and preserving a180day wait for applicants not otherwise eligible. Existing1254a(a)(1)(B)/(a)(2) authorizes employment throughout TPS. Document-validity clauses do not themselves terminate TPS, create first employment authority or establish individual eligibility. Existing1182(d)(5)(A)/(B) preserves case-by-case temporary humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole subject to the printed statutory exceptions, including its refugee qualification and the distinction from admission; paying a fee does not supply parole or work permission. Senate100016 requires a fiscal2025 fee of at least$5,000, or a higher DHS rule amount, on an alien BOTH ordered removed in absentia under1229a(b)(5) AND subsequently arrested by ICE, with fiscal2026-onward CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. It does not apply if the order was rescinded under1229a(b)(5)(C).50percent goes to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; the rest goes to Treasury. It expressly bars waiver/reduction. These fee conditions preserve the underlying notice/address/removability proof, rescission, exceptional-circumstances definition and motion-to-reopen stay in complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5)/(e) and1229(a); an actual order/arrest, new removal ground or denied legal review is not inferred. Senate100017 separately requires an additional fee from any INADMISSIBLE alien at the time the person is apprehended BETWEEN PORTS OF ENTRY. Its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or a higher DHS rule amount, with later CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. Unlike House70022, this operative sentence does not name CBP as the apprehending actor. It prints TWO proceeds clauses: subsection(c) sends50percent to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account for retention/spending without further appropriation and the remainder to Treasury; subsection(d) says ALL fees under the section go to Treasury. The exact EAS HTML and officialPDF pages827-828 both print these clauses. The candidate preserves the apparent allocation conflict and does not choose an operative distribution. No express no-waiver clause is printed in100017; do not import100016(e) or House70022(d), or infer that a waiver is available. These are exact between-port/inadmissibility and in-absentia-plus-ICE-arrest fee predicates, not all enforcement encounters or a fee-imposed finding that an alien actually met any predicate. Senate100004 adds a parole-entry fee with fiscal2025floor$1,000 or higher DHS rule amount, subsequent CPI-U increments rounded down to$10 and Treasury disposition. Its exceptions require the alien to establish the parole reason to DHS's satisfaction on an INDIVIDUAL,CASE-BY-CASE basis; its no-waiver clause expressly preserves those exceptions. The fee exceptions retain their actual predicates: a medical emergency with necessary treatment unavailable in the foreign state where the alien resides OR a life-threatening emergency with insufficient normal-visa time; the parent/legal guardian of such a medical-emergency MINOR; the alien needed in the US to donate an organ or tissue for transplant, with insufficient normal-visa time; a close family member in the United States whose death is imminent, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving while that person is alive; or seeking to attend a close family member's funeral, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving in the United States in time for it; an adopted child's urgent treatment needed before expected final adoption-related visa issuance while in the petitioner's legal custody; a LAWFUL INA245 adjustment applicant returning after temporary travel abroad; and a person returned to a contiguous country under235(b)(2)(C) paroled to attend the person's immigration hearing. The law-enforcement significant-public-benefit exception requires a DHS determination that significant public benefit has resulted or will result from the parole, BOTH assistance to the USGovernment AND presence required in that matter, PLUS at least one of inadmissibility, failure to meet nonimmigrant-admission eligibility, or insufficient normal-visa time; it is not every asserted public benefit. Senate exception9 instead requires that the alien HASBEENGRANTED the status of Cuban/Haitianentrant as defined inPL96-422Sec501(e). That complete definition distinguishes special Cuban/Haitianentrant-parole/subsequently-established special-status categories from OTHERCuban/Haitian nationals with the listed parole/no-other-status, removal-proceeding or pending-asylum alternatives AND no final,nonappealable,legally-enforceable removal order. Its status-at-assistance/services wording is preserved in the bound definition, not silently turned into proof of the fee-specific grant condition or a nationality-only exemption. Do not use the different House Cuba-residence/family-petition/program conjunction to define this replacement, or infer actual parole/fee exemption from nationality. Existing1182(d)(5) authority/statutory exceptions/non-admission distinction remain; paying or excepting a fee does not grant parole, admission or adjustment. Senate100005 requires an additional SIJapplication fee from ANYALIEN,PARENT,ORLEGALGUARDIAN of an alien applying under1101(a)(27)(J), with fiscal2025floor$250 or a higher DHS rule amount, later CPI increments rounded down to$10 and Treasury disposition. It does not print the House one-viable-parent fee predicate or the House express waiver bar; no waiver availability or separate cumulative charges on every named payer are inferred. Complete1101(a)(27)(J) retains the juvenile-court dependency/custody and1ORboth-parent nonviability findings, best-interest-against-return finding, DHSconsent, HHS-specific custody-jurisdiction consent and no derivative parentage rights. These fee provisions do not grant SIJstatus, import a UAC-under18 definition or alter those eligibility findings by themselves. Senate100006 edits EXISTING1254a(c)(1)(B) registration authority: it raises the statutory fee MAXIMUM from$50 to$500, subject to fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustments rounded down to$10. It leaves the existing AttorneyGeneral MAYrequire a REASONABLE registration fee language and separate work-document fee authority; this is not a mandatory universal$500charge, a$500minimum, the House conditional additional fee or the separate$550initial/$275renewal EADfees. The amendment adds Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction of required fees. The existing appropriation-credit sentence is NOTEXPRESSLYSTRUCK in the printed edit and remains in redesignatedclause(i), alongside addedclause(iii) directing all fees under the subparagraph to Treasury. Preserve that apparent proceeds interaction for legal/application review rather than silently deleting the baseline sentence or choosing an implemented distribution. The proposed registration-cap change does not grant or end TPS, guarantee status eligibility, prove payment or establish an individual's outcome. Senate 100007 adds a visa-integrity fee payable by any alien issued a nonimmigrant visa at issuance, in addition to other authorized fees. The fiscal 2025 minimum is $250 or a higher DHS rule amount; subsequent July-to-July CPI-U increments are rounded down to the nearest dollar. Unreimbursed fees go to Treasury and the applicable fee cannot be waived or reduced. DHS MAY reimburse after the visa period of validity expires only if the alien demonstrates compliance with ALL visa conditions after admission, including no unauthorized employment, AND one of two printed alternatives: (A) did not seek to extend the period of admission during the visa validity period AND departed no later than five days after the last day of "such period"; OR (B) during that validity period WAS GRANTED an extension of nonimmigrant status or adjustment to lawful permanent resident status. The text uses "such period" in alternative (A); its application is reserved rather than silently choosing visa validity or authorized admission as the referent. The House nonuse, filing-only and change-of-status alternatives are not imported into this version. A filing is not a grant; reimbursement remains discretionary and conditional, not guaranteed repayment or a general permission to stay/work. The complete pre-vote 1101(a)(26) definition distinguishes proper nonimmigrant visa issuance from actual admission, compliance or an individual outcome. Senate 100008 separately adds an I-94 application fee on any alien submitting that application, with fiscal 2025 minimum $24 or higher DHS rule amount, later July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to the nearest dollar and no waiver/reduction. Twenty percent of collected fees goes to the existing Land Border Inspection Fee Account pursuant to 1356(q)(2), available to CBP to retain and spend without further appropriation for I-94 processing; amounts not deposited there go to Treasury. The complete pre-vote subsection (q) establishes the account and its land-port receipt/expense/report framework. That baseline account scope is not substituted for the new section's any-alien I-94 application predicate, and its appropriations refunds are not applicant reimbursements. The visa fee and I-94 fee have separate collection events and dispositions; neither proves actual admission, visa compliance, a collection or immigration-status outcome. Senate 100014 amends the existing ESTA fee components under complete pre-vote1187(h)(3): the existing $17 per travel authorization remains, the separate full-System-cost-recovery component gains a $10 MINIMUM while retaining that cost condition, and a new component is at least $13 PER TRAVEL AUTHORIZATION. This does not describe a $10 or $13 total or first creation of ESTA. Its sunset edit extends the clause(i)(I) Travel Promotion Fund fee restriction from fiscal years beginning after October31,2028 to those beginning after October31,2034; it is not a sunset of every component. Its fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustment names the clause(i)(II) amount but literally uses the prior fee required UNDER THIS SUBPARAGRAPH as its base. That component/base relationship remains a separate application question, not a silently substituted isolated cost component or definite whole-fee adjustment; no increment-rounding rule is printed. Unlike selected House70017, this section does not edit existing clause(ii) disposition language: that baseline directs (i)(I) to the Travel Promotion Fund and (i)(II) to Treasury for System administration, but does not assign newly added (i)(III) by name. The new $13 component's disposition is separately reserved, without copying the House Treasury sentence or claiming to have closed other package funding provisions. Exact officialPDFpages819-821 visually confirm the printed adjustment language and section boundary; no HTML-parser repair is made. Existing travel-eligibility/admissibility/visa-eligibility distinctions remain, and no express new ESTA fee-waiver prohibition or inferred waiver availability is imported from EVUS. Senate 100015 separately adds an EVUS fee at enrollment for any alien SUBJECT to that System, additional to other authorized fees, with fiscal2025 minimum $30 or a higher DHS rule amount, later CPI-U increments rounded down to $0.25 and no waiver/reduction. It inserts a new1356(w) CBP EVUS Account with deposits equal to fees received MINUS $5 multiplied by the NUMBER OF PAYMENTS collected; that same $5-times-payments amount goes to Treasury. This payment-count language is retained rather than substituted with House70019's per-enrollment wording or inferred one-payment-per-enrollment implementation. Account amounts are appropriated without further appropriation and available until expended for CBP EVUS administration costs. OfficialPDF823 confirms the payment-count basis. The fee does not expand who is subject to EVUS, establish admission or visa/status eligibility, prove compliance or document an actual payment. Senate 100013 adds ten EOIR fee provisions despite its narrower adjustment-of-status section title. In either case, the claimed person must have attained 65 before the tax year closes and that person's defined SSN must be included on the return. One spouse's number alone does not establish deductions for both seniors. The amount is reduced, but not below zero, by 6 percent of modified adjusted gross income over $75,000, or over $150,000 on a joint return. If the taxpayer is married within the meaning of section 7703, this subparagraph applies only if the taxpayer and spouse file a joint return. The new House similar-32(d) provision and hypothetical-itemizer mechanism are not imported. This own deduction accompanies the extended zero-exemption/reference rules rather than replacing every existing aged standard amount or exempting all Social Security income. The inherited SSN definition is the same version's amended section 24(h)(7). It permits SSA issuance to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch, including the specified catch-up portion. In either case, the number must have been issued before the due date for the return. An ITIN or any other SSA number does not alone satisfy the definition, and the listed alien branch is not citizenship-only. The child-credit joint-return alternative does not replace the senior deduction's identification condition. Full marital authorities retain their own reference scopes and conditional separated-spouse rules; this description does not determine anyone's marital status. Complete section 63 preserves taxable-income and itemization mechanics and its own standard-deduction exclusions, including a nonresident alien individual. Section 151 retains its own spouse/exemption references and zero-exemption rule for other-provision deduction references. These are source-bound prerequisites, rather than eligibility for every alien, senior or itemizer or an accepted override of an exclusion. A deduction is not a dollar-for-dollar credit, an exemption of all Social Security benefits or a guaranteed refund. Both versions' senior amendments apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Each version retains its own printed limit for a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029. Both modified-income definitions add amounts excluded under sections 911, 931 and 933. No personal amount, return, age, marriage, residency or tax outcome is determined. Each adds its own mathematical-error omission reference: House (Z) names its section 63(f)(5)(D), while Senate (W) names its section 151(d)(5)(C). Those labels and provisions are not interchangeable. The inherited notice rules require an alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns a petition based on that notice. An abatement request may be filed within 60 days after the notice is sent. On receipt of that request the assessment must be abated, any reassessment uses deficiency procedures, and levy/court collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, fraud or loss of every remedy is inferred. Selected Senate section 70606 requires the individual's defined SSN on the return for both education credits. If the credit concerns qualified tuition and related expenses of an individual other than the taxpayer or spouse, that other individual's name and defined SSN are also required. For retention and signing bonuses, the Director shall provide each qualifying individual a written service agreement with its required period, amount, payment and early-termination terms. Transportation/related departure-removal costs, IT including fee collection, facilities/fleet, 287(g) agreements, VOICE staffing/nonfinancial victim assistance and OPLA immigration-enforcement/removal representation remain distinct purposes. Full material 287(g) limits, State/local expense and voluntary agreement/own no-agreement communication/cooperation paths remain; no blanket deputization, power or immunity. Victim-assistance perpetrator condition is not status-based guilt, cash for every victim or actual crime. Family paragraph (8) remains separately qualified. No actual hiring/bonus/agreement/collection/removal/expenditure or full-package closure.

Senate 100054 fiscal year 2025 $3.33 billion DOJ envelope through September 30, 2029 has separate selected EOIR, Byrne/COPS and incarceration purposes; neither all funds nor House earmarks are assigned to one. Senate 100054(2)/(3) drug/prosecution purposes use the shared $3.33 billion fiscal year 2025 envelope through September 30, 2029, without House earmarks. Own listed matters include unlawful voting; full 611 federal-office/exception/nonapplication predicates remain, no generic alien-guilt or new benefit/voting rule. Separate 100055 DOJ Fund. The Attorney General shall use the Fund amounts for grants to eligible States, State agencies, and units of local government, pursuant to their existing statutory authorities, for any of the following purposes. The paragraph 1 purpose is locating and apprehending aliens who have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. The paragraph 2 purpose is collection and analysis of law enforcement investigative information within the United States to counter gang or other criminal activity. The paragraph 3 purpose is investigating and prosecuting crimes committed by aliens within the United States and drug and human trafficking crimes committed within the United States. The paragraph 4 purpose is court operations related to the prosecution of crimes committed by aliens and drug and human trafficking crimes. The paragraph 5 purpose is temporary criminal detention of aliens. The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting aliens described in paragraph (1) within the United States to locations related to the apprehension, detention, and prosecution of such aliens. The paragraph 7 purpose is vehicle maintenance, logistics, transportation, and other support provided to law enforcement agencies by a State agency to enhance the ability to locate and apprehend aliens who have committed crimes under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. Paragraphs (1) and (7) retain their own additional-crime and unlawful-presence requirements; paragraph (6) retains the paragraph (1) person category, its domestic transport limit and its destination purposes. Those requirements are not imported into the other purposes. Temporary criminal detention is distinct from civil immigration detention. Court paragraph (4) prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase; no neighboring location condition is borrowed. Listed conjunctions report the source categories, not a determination that a particular grant must fund both crime categories. Existing statutory authorities do not create new State arrest/removal powers or establish actual crime/status/expense eligibility. Fiscal year 2025 appropriation is not to exceed $3,500,000,000 ($3.5 billion) until September 30, 2028, with qualified and documented expenses. The Attorney General may provide grants to State agencies and units of local government for their expenditures for completed, ongoing, or new activities determined to be eligible for such grant funding that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Amounts made available under this section shall be distributed to more than 1 State. No borrowed January 21 or 2029 date, automatic grant, actual crime/status/detention/hiring/spending or full-package closure. Existing question 46 subsection-scope application is unchanged.

Senate 100051(9)/(10) use the additional fiscal year 2025 $2,055,000,000 DHS envelope through September 30, 2029, in accordance with 235(b)(1)/(c), without House earmarks, House's express 212(a)(2)/(3) grounds wording or regardless-of-presence phrase. Senate 100051(8) and (11) are purposes within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. Neither purpose is a separate earmark for the full account, the ICE account or a House child appropriation. Paragraph (8) funds removal operations for specified unaccompanied alien children, but amounts under this paragraph shall only be used for permitting a specified unaccompanied alien child to withdraw the application for admission of the child pursuant to section 235(a)(4). The Secretary of Homeland Security must determine on a case-by-case basis all three specified-child conditions. First, the child has been found by an immigration officer at a land border or port of entry of the United States and is inadmissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Second, the child has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return of the child to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence. Third, the child does not have a fear of returning to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence owing to a credible fear of persecution. The paragraph does not print the House express contiguous-or-non-contiguous-country phrase or an independent-decision finding; neither is silently inserted into its definition. The incorporated unaccompanied-alien-child definition requires no lawful immigration status in the United States and not having attained 18 years of age, together with either no parent or legal guardian in the United States or no parent or legal guardian in the United States available to provide care and physical custody. The complete severe-forms-of-trafficking definition is bound with its own sex-trafficking and labor-or-services alternatives, force/fraud/coercion and under-18 distinctions; no label alone determines a child's eligibility. Paragraph (11) funds criminal and gang checks of defined unaccompanied alien children who are 12 years of age and older, including the examination of such unaccompanied alien children for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings. It prints no separate encountered-by-CBP condition; the House 70116 encounter condition is not imported. Its age-12 floor belongs to this check purpose, not the paragraph (8) withdrawal definition. Examination funding is not a finding that a child belongs to a gang, has committed a crime or is dangerous. Complete material captured pre-vote 235(a)(4) retains discretionary permission to withdraw and depart immediately, not a mandatory withdrawal or removal order. Complete TVPRA 235/1232 retains its own contiguous-child case-by-case trafficking/fear and independent-decision conditions, discretionary withdrawal/return, safe-return conditions, 48-hour screening and failed-or-undetermined-screen transfer, other-child custody pathway and own notification/72-hour-transfer exceptions. Its removal-proceedings, relief/access-to-counsel, placement, suitability and remaining safeguards retain their own scope. Senate funding does not itself establish their repeal, fulfillment or a universal individual return, protection or counsel outcome. Exact application interaction remains separate question 49; House question 43 is preserved independently.

Senate 100051(5) fingerprint and DNA purposes are within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 Secretary of Homeland Security account through September 30, 2029. Both purposes share the printed circumstance of aliens and alien children entering the United States without a valid visa. Subparagraph (A) funds collecting fingerprints, in accordance with section 262 and subsections (a)(3) and (b) of section 235 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Subparagraph (B) separately funds collecting DNA, in accordance with sections 235(d) and 287(b) of that Act. These are funding purposes with their own incorporated authorities, not a determination that every alien or child is subject to every collection power or that funded collection actually occurred. Captured 262(a) concerns an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is fourteen years of age or older, has not been registered and fingerprinted under section 1201(b) or section 30 or 31 of the Alien Registration Act, 1940, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer. All those conditions are common to its duty to apply for registration and to be fingerprinted before the expiration of such thirty days. Captured 262(b) separately requires a parent or legal guardian to apply for registration of an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is less than fourteen years of age, has not been registered under those named provisions, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer, before that period expires. That parent/guardian provision prints registration, not the same under-14 fingerprint duty. Whenever an alien attains his fourteenth birthday in the United States, the separate rule requires in-person registration and fingerprinting within thirty days thereafter. Captured 262(c) retains the Attorney General's discretionary nonimmigrant fingerprint waiver on the basis of reciprocity pursuant to prescribed regulations; no actual waiver is inferred. Complete 235(a)(3) concerns inspection of aliens, including crewmen, who apply for or otherwise seek admission, readmission or transit; it does not itself print a fingerprint command. Complete material 235(b)(1)/(2) screening, exceptions, asylum/fear/interview/review/consultation/detention and contiguous-return conditions remain bound, together with the original favorable-admission challenge. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 renumbers that original challenge from (3) to (4) and inserts the distinct State enforcement (3); the captured 2024 wording is not relabeled as an unamended 2025 subsection. Complete 235(d) retains its own belief-based conveyance search, detention/delivery with the alien-crewmember exception, named oath/evidence powers and subpoena-purpose/court-enforcement conditions. Complete 287(b) retains the designated officer/employee oath/evidence scope and its own knowing-or-willful false-evidence/perjury conditions. Neither cited provision expressly names DNA collection. That literal observation does not resolve whether other law, implementation rules or this funding language supports a proposed collection; question 50 reserves the exact DNA authority/application interaction. Question 51 separately reserves the fingerprint-purpose no-valid-visa circumstance alongside the incorporated registration age/prior-registration/duration/waiver paths and inspection procedures. No statutory repeal, guaranteed discretion outcome, universal biometric collection or actual child/parent/status/registration finding is inferred.

Remaining Senate 100051 purposes (1) through (4), (6), (7) and (12) share the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. They are purposes within that account, not separate full-envelope earmarks or borrowed ICE/House amounts. The paragraph 1 purpose is hiring and training of additional U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents, and the necessary support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities. The paragraph 2 purpose is funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with the departure or removal of aliens. The paragraph 3 purpose is funding for the assignment of Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement activities pursuant to sections 103(a) and 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 1357(g)). The paragraph 4 purpose is hiring additional staff and investing the necessary resources to enhance screening and vetting of all aliens seeking entry into United States, consistent with section 212 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1182), or intending to remain in the United States, consistent with section 237 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1227). The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting and facilitating the return, pursuant to section 235(b)(2)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(C)), of aliens arriving from contiguous territory. The paragraph 7 purpose is funding for State and local participation in homeland security efforts for purposes of: ending the presence of criminal gangs and criminal organizations throughout the United States; addressing crime and public safety threats; combating human smuggling and trafficking networks throughout the United States; supporting immigration enforcement activities; and providing reimbursement for State and local participation in such efforts. The paragraph 12 purpose is information technology investments to support immigration purposes, including improvements to fee and revenue collections. The entry and intended-remain screening categories retain their own section 212 and section 237 references. The State/local participation list retains all five own purposes, including its own throughout-the-United-States phrases. It does not borrow the reimbursement fund's crime-plus-unlawful-presence category or domestic transport restriction. The general departure/removal transportation purpose prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase. The assignment list retains Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers pursuant to both printed statutory references, not authority for any State employee to exercise all Federal powers. The printed purpose lists do not determine that a particular expenditure must fulfill every listed category. Fee and revenue collection IT is not a new fee, fine or penalty charge. Complete captured 103(a) retains its named agency roles, regulatory/delegation powers, consents and other conditions. In captured 103(a)(10), the Attorney General may authorize a State or local law enforcement officer to perform or exercise any of the powers, privileges, or duties conferred or imposed by this chapter or regulations issued thereunder upon officers or employees of the Service only in the event of the Attorney General's determination that an actual or imminent mass influx of aliens arriving off the coast of the United States, or near a land border, presents urgent circumstances requiring an immediate Federal response, and with the consent of the head of the department, agency, or establishment under whose jurisdiction the individual is serving. The captured event-specific authorization does not establish general unconditioned State power. Previously bound full 287(g) agreement qualifications, training, written powers/duration, Federal direction/supervision, voluntary/communication/cooperation and expense/employment/liability distinctions remain unchanged. Complete captured section 212(a) grounds and remaining operative section 212 authorities retain their own standards, exceptions, discretionary waivers and conditional notice rules, not an every-alien crime finding or guaranteed notice/waiver. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 replaces the original Attorney General references in 212(d)(5) with Secretary of Homeland Security and adds the distinct State enforcement route. Original captured 2024 words are preserved with that amending law, not relabeled as the complete unamended 2025 section. Complete captured section 237 retains distinct deportability grounds, actual conviction/knowledge/timing or other own requirements, exceptions/waivers, special nonimmigrant and SIJ boundaries and conditional administrative stays; screening funding does not determine an individual inadmissible, deportable or criminal. The contiguous-return purpose is pursuant to 235(b)(2)(C). The captured 235(b)(2)(C) return authority concerns an applicant for admission whom the examining immigration officer determines is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, arriving on land (whether or not at a designated port of arrival) from a foreign territory contiguous to the United States. The Attorney General may return that alien to that territory pending a proceeding under section 1229a. The captured parent exceptions for a crewman, an alien to whom paragraph (1) applies, and a stowaway remain. Discretionary return is not a final removal order or universal cross-border return duty. Complete captured 240 proceedings retain judge/charge/exclusive-procedure exceptions, own representation and evidence/examination limits, burdens, decision/appeal, motion and notice/deadline/stay rules. No guaranteed relief, government-paid counsel or individual hearing/return result is inferred. Other H.R.1 immigration components and separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

The Senate 90005(b) State Border Security Reinforcement Fund is a distinct DHS fund. Its complete selected operative clauses are retained below. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 1: There is established, in the Department of Homeland Security, a fund to be known as the ``State Border Security Reinforcement Fund.'' Senate 90005(b) paragraph 2: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts appropriated or otherwise made available for the Fund for grants to eligible States and units of local government for any of the following purposes: Senate 90005(b) purpose A: Construction or installation of a border wall, border fencing or other barrier, or buoys along the southern border of the United States, which may include planning, procurement of materials, and personnel costs related to such construction or installation. Senate 90005(b) purpose B: Any work necessary to prepare the ground at or near land borders to allow construction and maintenance of a border wall or other barrier fencing. Senate 90005(b) purpose C: Detection and interdiction of illicit substances and aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States and have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, and transfer or referral of such aliens to the Department of Homeland Security as provided by law. Senate 90005(b) purpose D: Relocation of aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States from small population centers to other domestic locations. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 3: In addition to amounts otherwise available for the purposes described in paragraph (2), there is appropriated for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to the Department of Homeland Security for the State Border Security Reinforcement Fund established by paragraph (1), $10,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2034, for qualified expenses for such purposes. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 4: The Secretary of Homeland Security may provide grants from the fund established by paragraph (1) to State agencies and units of local governments for expenditures made for completed, ongoing, or new activities, in accordance with law, that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 5: Each State desiring to apply for a grant under this subsection shall submit an application to the Secretary containing such information in support of the application as the Secretary may require. The Secretary shall require that each State include in its application the purposes for which the State seeks the funds and a description of how the State plans to allocate the funds. The Secretary shall begin to accept applications not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 6: Nothing in this subsection shall authorize any State or local government to exercise immigration or border security authorities reserved exclusively to the Federal Government under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) or the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). The Federal Emergency Management Agency may use not more than 1 percent of the funds made available under this subsection for the purpose of administering grants provided for in this section. The paragraph (2)(C) alien category retains both unlawful entry and commission of a crime under Federal, State, or local law; those alien predicates do not classify illicit substances. Transfer or referral remains as provided by law. Paragraph (2)(D) instead concerns unlawful presence and relocation from small population centers to other domestic locations; it does not borrow the crime or unlawful-entry predicates from (C), or authorize an international return. Only (A) specifies the southern border; (B) says at or near land borders. The paragraph (2) eligible-State/local-unit grant purpose rule and paragraph (4) discretionary State-agency/local-government expenditure rule remain distinct. The paragraph (5) application obligations name each State; no additional local-government obligation is inferred. The 90-day clause concerns when the Secretary must begin accepting applications, not an applicant deadline or a finding that applications are open. The paragraph (6) construction rule preserves exclusively Federal authorities without deciding which actual functions or expenditures fall within that reservation. The FEMA administration ceiling is discretionary, no more than 1 percent of funds under this subsection for grants in this section; its two scope words remain distinct. This is not an actual award, expenditure, eligibility, individual status/crime, relocation, power delegation or reimbursement determination. House reimbursement amounts, availability, January 21 date and duplicate-reimbursement restriction are not imported. Other package components and the 51 separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected Senate 90005(a) funding and its own program context follow. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 1: In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to be administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program authorized under section 2004 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605), to enhance State, local, and Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and other activities-- Senate 90005(a) purpose A: $500,000,000 for State and local capabilities to detect, identify, track, or monitor threats from unmanned aircraft systems (as such term is defined in section 44801 of title 49, United States Code), consistent with titles 18 and 49 of the United States Code; Senate 90005(a) purpose B: $625,000,000 for security and other costs related to the 2026 FIFA World Cup; Senate 90005(a) purpose C: $1,000,000,000 for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2028 Olympics; and Senate 90005(a) purpose D: $450,000,000 for the Operation Stonegarden Grant Program. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 2: None of the funds made available under subparagraph (B) or (C) of paragraph (1) shall be subject to the requirements of section 2004(e)(1) or section 2008(a)(12) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605(e)(1), 609(a)(12)). The pre-vote fiscal year 2024 DHS/FEMA HSGP notice reproduced on Hawaii's official host describes Operation Stonegarden as supporting enhanced cooperation and coordination among CBP, USBP, and Federal, State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to improve overall border security. It funds joint border-security efforts along routes of ingress and egress to and from international borders, including travel corridors in States bordering Mexico and Canada and States and territories with international water borders. In that notice, those State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies use their inherent law enforcement authorities and receive no additional authority from participating in Stonegarden. This is dated program-purpose context, not a new power conferred by the Senate appropriation or a complete 2025 eligibility rule. The additional fiscal year 2025 appropriation names FEMA Administrator, availability until September 30, 2029, administration under the State Homeland Security Grant Program in 6 U.S.C. 605, and State/local/Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements and other activities. The Stonegarden purpose is $450,000,000 within that administration provision. The drone-threat, FIFA and Olympics purposes retain their own printed objects and amounts as adjacent context; those purposes alone do not establish an immigration purpose. The exemption from 605(e)(1) minimum allocation and 609(a)(12) grant-administration expense cap expressly names only FIFA paragraph (1)(B) and Olympics paragraph (1)(C); no exemption for Stonegarden paragraph (1)(D) or drone paragraph (1)(A) is inferred. Captured 605(e)(1) retains its State and named-territory minimum-allocation branches, own fiscal-year denominators and percentages; captured 609(a)(12) permits expenses directly related to grant administration except that such expenses may not exceed 3 percent of the grant amount. Neither this cap nor those minima are reclassified as the separate 90005(b) FEMA one-percent ceiling. Complete captured 603, 605 and 609 retain their own program relationships, application/distribution/multistate rules, permitted-use and personnel/construction/recreation restrictions, waivers, reimbursement, transfers and equipment requirements. Their application to a particular 2025 Stonegarden award, including interaction with the dated 2024 notice's separate HSGP components and conditions, is reserved as question 52. No 2024 funding amount, application deadline, performance period, subrecipient tier or approval automatically governs this new appropriation. No particular State/local/Tribal award, entitlement, expenditure, additional law-enforcement power or individual status result is inferred. Other package components and all previously reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected exact Senate 70119 death/disability loan-discharge income-exclusion and SSN provisions follow. Senate 70119 exclusion grounds: In the case of an individual, gross income does not include any amount which (but for this subsection) would be includible in gross income for such taxable year by reason of the discharge (in whole or in part) of any loan described in subparagraph (B), if such discharge was-- (i) pursuant to subsection (a) or (d) of section 437 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 or the parallel benefit under part D of title IV of such Act (relating to the repayment of loan liability), (ii) pursuant to section 464(c)(1)(F) of such Act, or (iii) otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. Senate 70119 loan categories: A loan is described in this subparagraph if such loan is-- (i) a student loan (as defined in paragraph (2)), or (ii) a private education loan (as defined in section 140(a) of the Consumer Credit Protection Act (15 U.S.C. 1650(a)). Senate 70119 identification and own marital rules: (i) In general.--Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any discharge during any taxable year unless the taxpayer includes the taxpayer's social security number on the return of tax for such taxable year. (ii) Social security number.--For purposes of this subparagraph, the term `social security number' has the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7).. Senate 70119 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by this Act, is further amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (V), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (W) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (W) the following new subparagraph: (X) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 108(f)(5)(C) (relating to discharges on account of death or disability).. Senate 70119 discharge-date applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to discharges after December 31, 2025. Each version replaces only 108(f)(5) with the printed exclusion, not all of section 108 or every student-loan tax rule. The original 2024 (5) instead covers its defined discharge categories after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2026; the candidate does not silently extend that entire temporary rule unchanged. The common requirement that the discharged loan meet new subparagraph (B) applies across all three ground alternatives. Interaction of that gate, complete loan definitions and the parent-borrower 437(d) reference is reserved as question 55; no blanket conclusion that every HEA discharge qualifies for tax exclusion. Original (f)(1) service-conditioned discharge and (4) named repayment-program exclusions remain separate. New loan categories retain full 108(f)(2) student-loan definition and entire 140(a) private-education definitions, including actual (a)(8) private loan, own private-lender and expense meanings and excluded credit/mortgage categories. This does not mean every education-related debt qualifies. The three exclusion-ground alternatives remain separate: the first two use their specified HEA discharge paths, while only the third prints otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. A parent borrower is not silently equated to the student. Full 437(a) retains qualifying loans, death/disability determinations, safeguards, conditional reinstatement, VA documentation and own income-monitoring/approval/opt-out/update rules; 437(d) separately addresses a parent loan when the student dies. Captured 464(c)(1)(F) retains loan-fund agreement scope, borrower death, regulated permanent/total disability, the medically determinable substantial-gainful-activity alternative with its own duration/death tests, and VA unemployability due to service-connected disability. Part D parallel benefit is retained with complete captured 455 and its unless-otherwise-specified limitation, not a universal cancellation promise. Tax exclusion after a qualifying discharge is distinct from authority to cancel a loan. Both versions define the SSN by 24(h)(7), with their own same-bill amended definition and previously bound SSA issuance authority: citizen or the specified authorization route, and issuance before the return due date, not a bare identification number or a citizen-only rule. No child-credit amount or qualifying-child requirement is imported into the loan exclusion. Math-error treatment retains the existing notice and conditional abatement/deficiency procedure, including the 60-day abatement-request path; it is not a fraud finding or actual assessment. The effective date is discharges after December 31, 2025, not taxable years beginning after that date. No individual exclusion, discharge, marital status, SSA-number validity or return result is inferred. Senate requires the taxpayer SSN on the return and does not print the House conditional-spouse requirement or similar-32(d) addition. Those House clauses are not borrowed. Senate further amends the as-amended math-error list by adding (X), not House (W). House application question 54 is not treated as a settled Senate marital rule. Other H.R.1 components and all separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected exact Senate account and separate pilot eligibility clauses follow. Senate 70204 IRA treatment with own exceptions: Except as provided in this section or under regulations or guidance established by the Secretary, a Trump account shall be treated for purposes of this title in the same manner as an individual retirement account under section 408(a). Senate 70204 account establishment and instrument: The term `Trump account' means an individual retirement account (as defined in section 408(a)) which is not designated as a Roth IRA and which meets the following requirements: (A) The account-- (i) is created or organized by the Secretary for the exclusive benefit of an eligible individual or such eligible individual's beneficiaries, or (ii) is-- (I) created or organized in the United States for the exclusive benefit of an individual who has not attained the age of 18 before the end of the calendar year, or such individual's beneficiaries, and (II) funded by a qualified rollover contribution. (B) The account is designated (in such manner as the Secretary shall prescribe) at the time of the establishment of the account as a Trump account. (C) The written governing instrument creating the account meets the following requirements: (i) No contribution will be accepted-- (I) before the date that is 12 months after the date of the enactment of this section, or (II) in the case of a contribution made in any calendar year before the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18, if such contribution would result in aggregate contributions (other than exempt contributions) for such calendar year in excess of the contribution limit specified in subsection (c)(2)(A). (ii) Except as provided in subsection (d), no distribution will be allowed before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18. (iii) No part of the account funds will be invested in any asset other than an eligible investment during any period before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18.
