claim_source_map.passage: §1226. Apprehension and detention of aliens (a) Arrest, detention, and release On a warrant issued by the Attorney General, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States. Except as provided in subsection (c) and pending such decision, the Attorney General— (1) may continue to detain the arrested alien; and (2) may release the alien on— (A) bond of at least $1,500 with security approved by, and containing conditions prescribed by, the Attorney General; or (B) conditional parole; but (3) may not provide the alien with work authorization (including an "employment authorized" endorsement or other appropriate work permit), unless the alien is lawfully admitted for permanent residence or otherwise would (without regard to removal proceedings) be provided such authorization. (b) Revocation of bond or parole The Attorney General at any time may revoke a bond or parole authorized under subsection (a), rearrest the alien under the original warrant, and detain the alien. (c) Detention of criminal aliens (1) Custody The Attorney General shall take into custody any alien who— (A) is inadmissible by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1182(a)(2) of this title, (B) is deportable by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1227(a)(2)(A)(ii), (A)(iii), (B), (C), or (D) of this title, (C) is deportable under section 1227(a)(2)(A)(i) of this title on the basis of an offense for which the alien has been sentence 1 to a term of imprisonment of at least 1 year, or (D) is inadmissible under section 1182(a)(3)(B) of this title or deportable under section 1227(a)(4)(B) of this title, when the alien is released, without regard to whether the alien is released on parole, supervised release, or probation, and without regard to whether the alien may be arrested or imprisoned again for the same offense. (2) Release The Attorney General may release an alien described in paragraph (1) only if the Attorney General decides pursuant to section 3521 of title 18 that release of the alien from custody is necessary to provide protection to a witness, a potential witness, a person cooperating with an investigation into major criminal activity, or an immediate family member or close associate of a witness, potential witness, or person cooperating with such an investigation, and the alien satisfies the Attorney General that the alien will not pose a danger to the safety of other persons or of property and is likely to appear for any scheduled proceeding. A decision relating to such release shall take place in accordance with a procedure that considers the severity of the offense committed by the alien. (d) Identification of criminal aliens (1) The Attorney General shall devise and implement a system— (A) to make available, daily (on a 24-hour basis), to Federal, State, and local authorities the investigative resources of the Service to determine whether individuals arrested by such authorities for aggravated felonies are aliens; (B) to designate and train officers and employees of the Service to serve as a liaison to Federal, State, and local law enforcement and correctional agencies and courts with respect to the arrest, conviction, and release of any alien charged with an aggravated felony; and (C) which uses computer resources to maintain a current record of aliens who have been convicted of an aggravated felony, and indicates those who have been removed. (2) The record under paragraph (1)(C) shall be made available— (A) to inspectors at ports of entry and to border patrol agents at sector headquarters for purposes of immediate identification of any alien who was previously ordered removed and is seeking to reenter the United States, and (B) to officials of the Department of State for use in its automated visa lookout system. (3) Upon the request of the governor or chief executive officer of any State, the Service shall provide assistance to State courts in the identification of aliens unlawfully present in the United States pending criminal prosecution. (e) Judicial review The Attorney General's discretionary judgment regarding the application of this section shall not be subject to review. No court may set aside any action or decision by the Attorney General under this section regarding the detention or release of any alien or the grant, revocation, or denial of bond or parole.

claim_source_map.passage: (b) Inspection of applicants for admission (1) Inspection of aliens arriving in the United States and certain other aliens who have not been admitted or paroled (A) Screening (i) In general If an immigration officer determines that an alien (other than an alien described in subparagraph (F)) who is arriving in the United States or is described in clause (iii) is inadmissible under section 1182(a)(6)(C) or 1182(a)(7) of this title, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States without further hearing or review unless the alien indicates either an intention to apply for asylum under section 1158 of this title or a fear of persecution. (ii) Claims for asylum If an immigration officer determines that an alien (other than an alien described in subparagraph (F)) who is arriving in the United States or is described in clause (iii) is inadmissible under section 1182(a)(6)(C) or 1182(a)(7) of this title and the alien indicates either an intention to apply for asylum under section 1158 of this title or a fear of persecution, the officer shall refer the alien for an interview by an asylum officer under subparagraph (B). (iii) Application to certain other aliens (I) In general The Attorney General may apply clauses (i) and (ii) of this subparagraph to any or all aliens described in subclause (II) as designated by the Attorney General. Such designation shall be in the sole and unreviewable discretion of the Attorney General and may be modified at any time. (II) Aliens described An alien described in this clause is an alien who is not described in subparagraph (F), who has not been admitted or paroled into the United States, and who has not affirmatively shown, to the satisfaction of an immigration officer, that the alien has been physically present in the United States continuously for the 2-year period immediately prior to the date of the determination of inadmissibility under this subparagraph. (B) Asylum interviews (i) Conduct by asylum officers An asylum officer shall conduct interviews of aliens referred under subparagraph (A)(ii), either at a port of entry or at such other place designated by the Attorney General. (ii) Referral of certain aliens If the officer determines at the time of the interview that an alien has a credible fear of persecution (within the meaning of clause (v)), the alien shall be detained for further consideration of the application for asylum. (iii) Removal without further review if no credible fear of persecution (I) In general Subject to subclause (III), if the officer determines that an alien does not have a credible fear of persecution, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States without further hearing or review. (II) Record of determination The officer shall prepare a written record of a determination under subclause (I). Such record shall include a summary of the material facts as stated by the applicant, such additional facts (if any) relied upon by the officer, and the officer's analysis of why, in the light of such facts, the alien has not established a credible fear of persecution. A copy of the officer's interview notes shall be attached to the written summary. (III) Review of determination The Attorney General shall provide by regulation and upon the alien's request for prompt review by an immigration judge of a determination under subclause (I) that the alien does not have a credible fear of persecution. Such review shall include an opportunity for the alien to be heard and questioned by the immigration judge, either in person or by telephonic or video connection. Review shall be concluded as expeditiously as possible, to the maximum extent practicable within 24 hours, but in no case later than 7 days after the date of the determination under subclause (I). (IV) Mandatory detention Any alien subject to the procedures under this clause shall be detained pending a final determination of credible fear of persecution and, if found not to have such a fear, until removed. (iv) Information about interviews The Attorney General shall provide information concerning the asylum interview described in this subparagraph to aliens who may be eligible. An alien who is eligible for such interview may consult with a person or persons of the alien's choosing prior to the interview or any review thereof, according to regulations prescribed by the Attorney General. Such consultation shall be at no expense to the Government and shall not unreasonably delay the process. (v) "Credible fear of persecution" defined For purposes of this subparagraph, the term "credible fear of persecution" means that there is a significant possibility, taking into account the credibility of the statements made by the alien in support of the alien's claim and such other facts as are known to the officer, that the alien could establish eligibility for asylum under section 1158 of this title. (C) Limitation on administrative review Except as provided in subparagraph (B)(iii)(III), a removal order entered in accordance with subparagraph (A)(i) or (B)(iii)(I) is not subject to administrative appeal, except that the Attorney General shall provide by regulation for prompt review of such an order under subparagraph (A)(i) against an alien who claims under oath, or as permitted under penalty of perjury under section 1746 of title 28, after having been warned of the penalties for falsely making such claim under such conditions, to have been lawfully admitted for permanent residence, to have been admitted as a ref ugee under section 1157 of this title, or to have been granted asylum under section 1158 of this title. (D) Limit on collateral attacks In any action brought against an alien under section 1325(a) of this title or section 1326 of this title, the court shall not have jurisdiction to hear any claim attacking the validity of an order of removal entered under subparagraph (A)(i) or (B)(iii). (E) "Asylum officer" defined As used in this paragraph, the term "asylum officer" means an immigration officer who— (i) has had professional training in country conditions, asylum law, and interview techniques comparable to that provided to full-time adjudicators of applications under section 1158 of this title, and (ii) is supervised by an officer who meets the condition described in clause (i) and has had substantial experience adjudicating asylum applications. (F) Exception Subparagraph (A) shall not apply to an alien who is a native or citizen of a country in the Western Hemisphere with whose government the United States does not have full diplomatic relations and who arrives by aircraft at a port of entry. (G) Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to authorize or require any person described in section 1158(e) of this title to be permitted to apply for asylum under section 1158 of this title at any time before January 1, 2014. (2) Inspection of other aliens (A) In general Subject to subparagraphs (B) and (C), in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained for a proceeding under section 1229a of this title. (B) Exception Subparagraph (A) shall not apply to an alien— (i) who is a crewman, (ii) to whom paragraph (1) applies, or (iii) who is a stowaway. (C) Treatment of aliens arriving from contiguous territory In the case of an alien described in subparagraph (A) who is arriving on land (whether or not at a designated port of arrival) from a foreign territory contiguous to the United States, the Attorney General may return the alien to that territory pending a proceeding under section 1229a of this title.

claim_source_map.passage: (a) Detention, release, and removal of aliens ordered removed (1) Removal period (A) In general Except as otherwise provided in this section, when an alien is ordered removed, the Attorney General shall remove the alien from the United States within a period of 90 days (in this section referred to as the "removal period"). (B) Beginning of period The removal period begins on the latest of the following: (i) The date the order of removal becomes administratively final. (ii) If the removal order is judicially reviewed and if a court orders a stay of the removal of the alien, the date of the court's final order. (iii) If the alien is detained or confined (except under an immigration process), the date the alien is released from detention or confinement. (C) Suspension of period The removal period shall be extended beyond a period of 90 days and the alien may remain in detention during such extended period if the alien fails or refuses to make timely application in good faith for travel or other documents necessary to the alien's departure or conspires or acts to prevent the alien's removal subject to an order of removal. (2) Detention During the removal period, the Attorney General shall detain the alien. Under no circumstance during the removal period shall the Attorney General release an alien who has been found inadmissible under section 1182(a)(2) or 1182(a)(3)(B) of this title or deportable under section 1227(a)(2) or 1227(a)(4)(B) of this title.

claim_source_map.passage: (f) Limit on injunctive relief (1) In general Regardless of the nature of the action or claim or of the identity of the party or parties bringing the action, no court (other than the Supreme Court) shall have jurisdiction or authority to enjoin or restrain the operation of the provisions of part IV of this subchapter, as amended by the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, other than with respect to the application of such provisions to an individual alien against whom proceedings under such part have been initiated. (2) Particular cases Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no court shall enjoin the removal of any alien pursuant to a final order under this section unless the alien shows by clear and convincing evidence that the entry or execution of such order is prohibited as a matter of law.

claim_source_map.passage:
(a)(1) The Attorney General may provide for the relocation and other protection of a witness or a potential witness for the Federal Government or for a State government in an official proceeding concerning an organized criminal activity or other serious offense, if the Attorney General determines that an offense involving a crime of violence directed at the witness with respect to that proceeding, an offense set forth in chapter 73 of this title directed at the witness, or a State offense that is similar in nature to either such offense, is likely to be committed. The Attorney General may also provide for the relocation and other protection of the immediate family of, or a person otherwise closely associated with, such witness or potential witness if the family or person may also be endangered on account of the participation of the witness in the judicial proceeding. (2) The Attorney General shall issue guidelines defining the types of cases for which the exercise of the authority of the Attorney General contained in paragraph (1) would be appropriate. (3) The United States and its officers and employees shall not be subject to any civil liability on account of any decision to provide or not to provide protection under this chapter. 

(c) Before providing protection to any person under this chapter, the Attorney General shall, to the extent practicable, obtain information relating to the suitability of the person for inclusion in the program, including the criminal history, if any, and a psychological evaluation of, the person. The Attorney General shall also make a written assessment in each case of the seriousness of the investigation or case in which the person's information or testimony has been or will be provided and the possible risk of danger to other persons and property in the community where the person is to be relocated and shall determine whether the need for that person's testimony outweighs the risk of danger to the public. In assessing whether a person should be provided protection under this chapter, the Attorney General shall consider the person's criminal record, alternatives to providing protection under this chapter, the possibility of securing similar testimony from other sources, the need for protecting the person, the relative importance of the person's testimony, results of psychological examinations, whether providing such protection will substantially infringe upon the relationship between a child who would be relocated in connection with such protection and that child's parent who would not be so relocated, and such other factors as the Attorney General considers appropriate. The Attorney General shall not provide protection to any person under this chapter if the risk of danger to the public, including the potential harm to innocent victims, outweighs the need for that person's testimony. This subsection shall not be construed to authorize the disclosure of the written assessment made pursuant to this subsection. (d)(1) Before providing protection to any person under this chapter, the Attorney General shall enter into a memorandum of understanding with that person. Each such memorandum of understanding shall set forth the responsibilities of that person, including— (A) the agreement of the person, if a witness or potential witness, to testify in and provide information to all appropriate law enforcement officials concerning all appropriate proceedings; (B) the agreement of the person not to commit any crime; (C) the agreement of the person to take all necessary steps to avoid detection by others of the facts concerning the protection provided to that person under this chapter; (D) the agreement of the person to comply with legal obligations and civil judgments against that person; (E) the agreement of the person to cooperate with all reasonable requests of officers and employees of the Government who are providing protection under this chapter; (F) the agreement of the person to designate another person to act as agent for the service of process; (G) the agreement of the person to make a sworn statement of all outstanding legal obligations, including obligations concerning child custody and visitation; (H) the agreement of the person to disclose any probation or parole responsibilities, and if the person is on probation or parole under State law, to consent to Federal supervision in accordance with section 3522 of this title; and (I) the agreement of the person to regularly inform the appropriate program official of the activities and current address of such person. Each such memorandum of understanding shall also set forth the protection which the Attorney General has determined will be provided to the person under this chapter, and the procedures to be followed in the case of a breach of the memorandum of understanding, as such procedures are established by the Attorney General. Such procedures shall include a procedure for filing and resolution of grievances of persons provided protection under this chapter regarding the administration of the program. This procedure shall include the opportunity for resolution of a grievance by a person who was not involved in the case. (2) The Attorney General shall enter into a separate memorandum of understanding pursuant to this subsection with each person protected under this chapter who is eighteen years of age or older. The memorandum of understanding shall be signed by the Attorney General and the person protected. (3) The Attorney General may delegate the responsibility initially to authorize protection under this chapter only to the Deputy Attorney General, to the Associate Attorney General, to any Assistant Attorney General in charge of the Criminal Division or National Security Division of the Department of Justice, to the Assistant Attorney General in charge of the Civil Rights Division of the Department of Justice (insofar as the delegation relates to a criminal civil rights case), and to one other officer or employee of the Department of Justice. (e) If the Attorney General determines that harm to a person for whom protection may be provided under section 3521 of this title is imminent or that failure to provide immediate protection would otherwise seriously jeopardize an ongoing investigation, the Attorney General may provide temporary protection to such person under this chapter before making the written assessment and determination required by subsection (c) of this section or entering into the memorandum of understanding required by subsection (d) of this section. In such a case the Attorney General shall make such assessment and determination and enter into such memorandum of understanding without undue delay after the protection is initiated.

findings.compact: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.495 to add annual implementation reports on the existing cross-border-tunnel strategic plan. H.R.495 would add annual CBP reports on implementation of the existing illicit cross-border-tunnel strategic plan after its initial report deadline; it does not newly establish that plan or authorize additional funding.
detail: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.495 to add annual implementation reports on the existing cross-border-tunnel strategic plan.

The exact H.R.495 EH proposal adds “and annually thereafter” to Public Law 117-263 section 7134(a)(2), after “development of the strategic plan”. The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection would therefore report on implementation of the existing counter illicit cross-border tunnel operations strategic plan not later than one year after its development and annually thereafter, to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The separate 6 USC 257 annual report on discovered Mexico–U.S. tunnels and DHS prevention/investigation/prosecution needs already exists and is not the provision amended here. Existing 7134(b) authorized$1 million for each of fiscal 2023 and 2024 for plan development and remediation; H.R.495 neither extends that authorization nor supplies new appropriations. Membership follows direct border-tunnel operations reporting. Actual reporting, tunnel remediation, border outcomes or enactment are not established by the House suspension-and-passage vote.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-03-10. This does not establish enactment.

findings.headline: H.R.993 border-technology plan and innovation-team authority
findings.compact: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.993 with its border-technology planning, innovation-team authority and procedures/reporting. H.R.993 would require a 180-day border-technology plan, authorize CBP innovation teams to research/adapt emerging commercial technologies, and require team procedures, metrics and reports; it does not require universal deployment or appropriate funds.
detail: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.993 with its border-technology planning, innovation-team authority and procedures/reporting.

The exact H.R.993 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, acting through the CBP Commissioner and DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary, to submit a plan within 180 days of enactment to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The plan is to identify, integrate and deploy emerging/advanced technologies to enhance or address gaps in border-security operations. Its prescribed contents cover innovation-team use and composition, contributions and coordination, technologies from other agencies, procurement authorities and need for alternatives, scaling programs, program goals/timelines, border-community privacy/security impacts, replacement costs, research/private-sector coordination, metrics and listed aircraft/surveillance/inspection/tunnel/communications technologies. The bill gives the CBP Commissioner express authority to maintain one or more innovation teams to research and adapt new/emerging commercial technologies for border capability gaps and urgent mission needs, and assess potential outcomes including negative consequences where documented gaps are yet to be determined. It requires each maintained team to establish operating procedures, defined roles/partner relationships and transition protocols, plus strategic planning with costs, timeframes, metrics and performance parameters, including technology-transition rates. The Commissioner must report within 180 days and annually thereafter to the same committees on team procedures/plans, technologies piloted in the preceding fiscal year, success/gap determinations and status of transitioning successful technologies. This provides statutory authority and prescribed planning/reporting for maintaining teams; it does not establish that innovation teams or pilots first come into existence with this proposal. The technology list and planned deployment goals are not universal mandates to deploy every technology. No appropriation, universal pilot success or actual operational outcome is stated. Membership follows the express direct border-operations scope rather than DHS administration alone.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-03-10. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The 180-day plan submission is assigned to the DHS Secretary through the CBP Commissioner and Science and Technology Under Secretary. The separate 180-day/annual team report is assigned to the Commissioner; both go to the two specified Homeland Security committees.

Team maintenance is authorized rather than mandatory creation of a particular number. Operating procedures/plans are required for maintained teams; their authority includes research/adaptation and assessing possible negative outcomes even before documented gaps are determined.

Plan contents include privacy/security impacts on border communities, procurement-authority analysis, cost estimates, timeframes and transition metrics. The list of technologies is not an order to deploy every technology, and reports on pilots are not proof of successful or universal deployment.

The bill supplies statutory team authority and planning/reporting requirements, not a claim that teams are historically new. It does not provide appropriations or establish actual spending, procurement, deployment, effectiveness or enactment.

This exact suspension-and-passage vote concerns the complete bill. It does not establish separate preferences about artificial intelligence, surveillance, individual technologies or any plan component.

claim_source_map.locator: Section 2(a)-(b): actors,180-day plan and all required contents
claim_source_map.passage: (a) In General.--Not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Homeland Security, acting through the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Under Secretary for Science and Technology of the Department of Homeland Security, shall submit to the Committee on Homeland Security of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs of the Senate a plan to identify, integrate, and deploy new, innovative, disruptive, or other emerging or advanced technologies that may incorporate artificial intelligence, machine- learning, automation, fiber-optic sensing technology, nanotechnology, optical and cognitive radar, modeling and simulation technology, hyperspectral and LIDAR sensors, imaging, identification, and categorization systems, or other emerging or advanced technologies, to enhance, or address capability gaps in, border security operations. (b) Contents.--The plan required under subsection (a) shall include the following: (1) Information regarding how CBP utilizes CBP Innovation Team authority under subsection (c) and other mechanisms to carry out the purposes specified in subsection (a). (2) An assessment of the contributions directly attributable to such utilization. (3) Information regarding the composition of each CBP Innovation Team, and how each such Team coordinates and integrates efforts with the CBP acquisition program office and other partners within CBP and the Department of Homeland Security. (4) Identification of technologies used by other Federal departments or agencies not in use by CBP that could assist in enhancing, or addressing capability gaps in, border security operations. (5) An analysis of authorities available to CBP to procure technologies referred to subsection (a), and an assessment as to whether additional or alternative authorities are needed to carry out the purposes specified in such subsection. (6) An explanation of how CBP plans to scale existing programs related to emerging or advanced technologies into programs of record. (7) A description of each planned security-related technology program, including objectives, goals, and timelines for each such program. (8) An assessment of the privacy and security impact on border communities of security-related technology. (9) An assessment of CBP legacy border technology programs that could be phased out and replaced by technologies referred to in subsection (a), and cost estimates relating to such phase out and replacement. (10) Information relating to how CBP is coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security's Science and Technology Directorate to carry out the following: (A) Research and develop new, innovative, disruptive, or other emerging or advanced technologies to carry out the purposes specified in subsection (a). (B) Identify security-related technologies that are in development or deployed by the private and public sectors that may satisfy the mission needs of CBP, with or without adaptation. (C) Incentivize the private sector to develop technologies that may help CBP meet mission needs to enhance, or address capability gaps in, border security operations. (D) Identify and assess ways to increase opportunities for communication and collaboration with the private sector, small and disadvantaged businesses, intra-governmental entities, university centers of excellence, and Federal laboratories to leverage emerging technology and research within the public and private sectors. (11) Information on metrics and key performance parameters for evaluating the effectiveness of efforts to identify, integrate, and deploy new, innovative, disruptive, or other emerging or advanced technologies to carry out the purposes specified in subsection (a). (12) An identification of recent technological advancements in the following: (A) Manned aircraft sensor, communication, and common operating picture technology. (B) Unmanned aerial systems and related technology, including counter-unmanned aerial system technology. (C) Surveillance technology, including the following: (i) Mobile surveillance vehicles. (ii) Associated electronics, including cameras, sensor technology, and radar. (iii) Tower-based surveillance technology. (iv) Advanced unattended surveillance sensors. (v) Deployable, lighter-than-air, ground surveillance equipment. (D) Nonintrusive inspection technology, including non-X-ray devices utilizing muon tomography and other advanced detection technology. (E) Tunnel detection technology. (F) Communications equipment, including the following: (i) Radios. (ii) Long-term evolution broadband. (iii) Miniature satellites. (13) Any other information the Secretary determines relevant.

findings.headline: H.R.23 conditional ICC-related immigration sanctions
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.23 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established. H.R.23 would require conditional ICC-related sanctions, including visa/admission/parole and other INA-benefit restrictions and immediate entry-document revocation for designated foreign actors and specified immediate relatives, subject to waiver and termination provisions.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.23 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established.

The exact House-passed H.R.23 requires the President, not later than 60 days after enactment and on an ongoing basis, to impose sanctions if the ICC is attempting to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute a protected person. Covered foreign persons are those the President determines directly engage in or aid such an effort; materially assist, sponsor or provide specified support/goods/services for it; or are owned/controlled by, or currently act or purport to have acted for, a person directly engaging in it. For covered aliens, the bill makes them inadmissible, ineligible for visas or other entry documents, admission or parole, and any other INA benefit. Their visas/entry documents must be revoked regardless of issuance date, effective immediately and automatically canceling other valid visas/entry documents in their possession. The immigration sanctions also apply to each sanctioned foreign person's spouse, parent, sibling or adult child; the separate property-blocking requirement applies to the principal foreign persons described in 3(a)(1). Foreign person means someone other than the defined United States person, which includes U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities and any person in the United States. The incorporated INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals. Protected persons include any defined U.S. person unless the United States both formally consents to ICC jurisdiction and is a Rome Statute party. They also include foreign citizens or lawful residents of a NATO or designated major non-NATO ally that has not consented to ICC jurisdiction or is not a Rome Statute party. The listed military/government personnel are inclusive examples, not the entire protected class. The President may waive sanctions case by case for periods no longer than 90 days each on a reported vital-national-security determination before the waiver takes effect, including the specified detailed rationale and actions by the United States and ICC. The President may terminate sanctions on written certification that the ICC has ceased all covered efforts and permanently closed/withdrawn/ended/terminated them. Imposition also requires congressional briefing/written notice within 10 days. The package includes property blocking under existing IEEPA authorities and penalties, rescission of available ICC appropriations at enactment and a prospective ban on using appropriated funds for the ICC. Immigration membership follows the direct travel/admission/parole/benefit restrictions, not the foreign-affairs findings. These are proposed legislative requirements; existing general INA inadmissibility/temporary-admission authorities are not treated as newly created by this bill. Actual designation, visa revocation, sanctions, enforcement or enactment is not inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-09. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The trigger is an ICC attempt against a defined protected person plus the President's specified actor determination. It is not an unconditional travel ban on every ICC employee or foreign national. Protected-person conditions distinguish U.S. persons from citizens/lawful residents of defined allies.

Immediate relatives mean spouse, parent, sibling or adult child. Immigration sanctions extend to relatives who meet the INA alien definition; the principal-target foreign-person limitation is not assumed to exclude every lawful-permanent-resident relative. Property blocking in 3(b)(1) refers to the principal 3(a)(1) actors.
Visa/entry-document revocation is immediate and cancels other valid entry documents regardless of issuance date. No individual designation or actual entry refusal is established by a House vote.

Waivers are case by case, at most 90 days each, with a vital-national-security determination and a specified pre-effect congressional report. Termination requires written certification of both cessation and permanent ending of all protected-person efforts; ordinary general INA discretion is not substituted for this specific sanctions waiver.

This is whole-bill passage with property/funding provisions as well as immigration sanctions. It does not establish separate approval of each component, endorse the bill's findings, or establish actual spending, sanctioning, revocation or enactment.

claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 3. SANCTIONS WITH RESPECT TO THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT. (a) In General.--Not later than 60 days after the date of enactment of this Act, and on an ongoing basis thereafter, if the International Criminal Court is engaging in any attempt to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute any protected person, the President shall impose-- (1) the sanctions described in subsection (b) with respect to any foreign person the President determines-- (A) has directly engaged in or otherwise aided any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; (B) has materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; or (C) is owned or controlled by, or is currently acting or purports to have acted, directly or indirectly, for or on behalf of any person that directly engages in any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; and (2) the sanctions described in subsection (b)(2) with respect to the immediate family members of each foreign person who is subject to sanctions pursuant to paragraph (1). (b) Sanctions Described.--The sanctions described in this subsection with respect to a foreign person described in subsection (a) are the following: (1) Property blocking.--The President shall exercise all of the powers granted by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) to the extent necessary to block and prohibit all transactions in all property and interests in property of any foreign person described in subsection (a)(1) if such property and interests in property are in the United States, come within the United States, or are or come within the possession or control of a United States person. (2) Aliens inadmissible for visas, admission, or parole.-- (A) Visas, admission, or parole.--In the case of an alien described in subsection (a), the alien is-- (i) inadmissible to the United States; (ii) ineligible to receive a visa or other documentation to enter the United States; and (iii) otherwise ineligible to be admitted or paroled into the United States or to receive any other benefit under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.). (B) Current visas revoked.-- (i) In general.--The visa or other entry documentation of an alien described in subparagraph (A) shall be revoked, regardless of when such visa or other entry documentation was issued. (ii) Immediate effect.--A revocation under clause (i) shall-- (I) take effect immediately; and (II) automatically cancel any other valid visa or entry documentation that is in the alien's possession.

claim_source_map.locator: Section 3(c)–(f): implementation, notification, waiver and termination
claim_source_map.passage: (c) Implementation; Penalties.-- (1) Implementation.--The President may exercise all authorities provided under sections 203 and 205 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704) to carry out this section. (2) Penalties.--A person that violates, attempts to violate, conspires to violate, or causes a violation of this section or any regulation, license, or order issued to carry out this section shall be subject to the penalties set forth in subsections (b) and (c) of section 206 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1705) to the same extent as a person that commits an unlawful act described in subsection (a) of that section. (d) Notification to Congress.--Not later than 10 days after any imposition of sanctions pursuant to subsection (a), the President shall brief and provide written notification to the appropriate congressional committees regarding the imposition of sanctions that shall include-- (1) a description of the foreign person or persons subject to the imposition of such sanctions, including the foreign person's role at or relation to the International Criminal Court; (2) a description of any activity undertaken by such foreign person or persons in support of efforts to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute any protected person; and (3) the specific sanctions imposed on such foreign person or persons. (e) Waiver.-- (1) In general.--The President may, on a case-by-case basis and for periods not to exceed 90 days each, waive the application of sanctions imposed or maintained with respect to a foreign person under this section if the President submits to the appropriate congressional committees before the waiver is to take effect a report that contains a determination of the President that the waiver is vital to the national security interests of the United States. (2) Contents.--Each report required by paragraph (1) with respect to a waiver of the application of sanctions imposed or maintained with respect to a foreign person under this section, or the renewal of such a waiver, shall include-- (A) a specific and detailed rationale for the determination that the waiver is vital to the national security interests of the United States; (B) a description of the activity that resulted in the foreign person being subject to sanctions; (C) a detailed description and list of actions the United States has taken to stop the International Criminal Court from engaging in any effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons; and (D) a detailed description and list of actions the International Criminal Court has taken to permanently close, withdraw, end, or otherwise terminate any preliminary examination, investigation, or any other effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons. (3) Form.--Each report required by paragraph by paragraph (1) shall be submitted in unclassified form but may include a classified annex. (f) Special Rule.--The President may terminate the sanctions with respect to the foreign persons described in subsection (a) if the President certifies in writing to the appropriate congressional committees that the International Criminal Court-- (1) has ceased engaging in any effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons; and (2) has permanently closed, withdrawn, ended, and otherwise terminated any preliminary examination, investigation, or any other effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons.

claim_source_map.locator: Sections 4–5: package funding provisions and all actor/protected-person definitions
claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 4. RESCISSION OF FUNDS FOR INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT. (a) In General.--Effective on the date of the enactment of this Act, any amounts appropriated for the International Criminal Court and available for obligation as of such date of enactment are hereby rescinded. (b) Prohibition on Future Appropriations.--On and after the date of the enactment of this Act, no appropriated funds may be used for the International Criminal Court. SEC. 5. DEFINITIONS. In this Act: (1) Admitted alien.--The terms ``admitted'' and ``alien'' have the meanings given those terms in section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101). (2) Ally of the united states.--The term ``ally of the United States'' means-- (A) a government of a member country of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; or (B) a government of a major non-NATO ally, as that term is defined by section 2013(7) of the American Service-Members' Protection Act (22 U.S.C. 7432(7)). (3) Appropriate congressional committees defined.--The term ``appropriate congressional committees'' means-- (A) the Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Committee on Financial Services, and the Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives; and (B) the Committee on Foreign Relations the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and the Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate. (4) Foreign person.--The term ``foreign person'' means a person that is not a United States person. (5) Immediate family member.--The term ``immediate family member'', with respect to a foreign person, means the spouse, parent, sibling, or adult child of the person. (6) International criminal court; rome statute.--The terms ``International Criminal Court'' and ``Rome Statute'' have the meaning given those terms in section 2013 of the American Service-Members' Protection Act (22 U.S.C. 7432). (7) Protected person.--The term ``protected person'' means-- (A) any United States person, unless the United States provides formal consent to International Criminal Court jurisdiction and is a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, including-- (i) current or former members of the Armed Forces of the United States; (ii) current or former elected or appointed officials of the United States Government; and (iii) any other person currently or formerly employed by or working on behalf of the United States Government; (B) any foreign person that is a citizen or lawful resident of an ally of the United States that has not consented to International Criminal Court jurisdiction or is not a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, including-- (i) current or former members of the Armed Forces of such ally of the United States; (ii) current or former elected or appointed government officials of such ally of the United States; and (iii) any other person currently or formerly employed by or working on behalf of such a government. (8) United states person.--The term ``United States person'' means-- (A) an individual who is a United States citizen or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence to the United States; (B) an entity organized under the laws of the United States or any jurisdiction within the United States, including a foreign branch of such an entity; or (C) any person in the United States.

findings.headline: H.R. 1968 package with selected Immigration funding, safeguards, refugee and adjustment provisions
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of that complete H.R. 1968 package; no separate position on a funding account, safeguard, refugee, adjustment or other component, or preferred alternative, is established. H.R. 1968 continues selected border and immigration-service funding and custody safeguards, includes qualified refugee-rule and inspection/parole-window extensions and an Afghan heading edit, and incorporates qualified employment and visa program rules with reserved timing questions. Other Immigration components remain under review; the vote concerns the whole package.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of that complete H.R. 1968 package; no separate position on a funding account, safeguard, refugee, adjustment or other component, or preferred alternative, is established.

The exact March 11, 2025 House choice is passage of the complete H.R. 1968 continuing-appropriations and extensions package. The selected, separately source-bound Immigration mechanisms here include DHS funding and retained safeguards, division A section 11208(a) refugee and adjustment date amendments, the separate section 11208(b) Afghan-program heading amendment, and incorporated physician, E-Verify, religious-worker and H-2B rules with reserved timing application. Other Immigration components of the package remain under review; this candidate does not claim complete component coverage.

Section 11208(a)(1) would add fiscal year 2025 to section 599D(b)(3). Within refugee admissions already allocated under section 207(a)(3) for nationals of the independent states of the former Soviet Union, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the President must allocate one thousand admissions to the narrower section 599D(b)(2)(B) recipient category. That category consists of people who are or were nationals of those countries, are current members of the Ukrainian Catholic Church or Ukrainian Orthodox Church, and demonstrate public, active and continuous participation (or attempted participation) in the religious activities of that church. The larger nationality-based admissions allocation and this narrower religious recipient category are distinct. It is not an extra one thousand outside the allocated admissions ceiling, and it does not increase the general refugee admission ceiling. Replacing 2024 with 2025 in all three section 599D(e) branches would carry forward the special category-based fear showing (asserting a well-founded fear and a credible basis for concern about possible persecution) for applications submitted before October 1, 2025, the written-reasons requirement to the maximum extent feasible for decisions made before that date, and the specified previously denied applicants' reapplication route before that date. The complete baseline keeps its distinct former-Soviet/Baltic, Vietnam/Laos/Cambodia and Iranian religious-minority category definitions and other refugee admission qualifications. Neither country membership alone nor a reduced fear-showing rule guarantees admission.

Section 11208(a)(2) would change the section 599E(b)(2) qualifying inspection-and-parole window's ending date from September 30, 2024 to September 30, 2025, retaining the August 15, 1988 starting date. Its separate national list covers former-Soviet states, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia; the Iranian category in 599D is not imported into this adjustment route. The person must have been denied refugee status before the qualifying inspection and parole, apply for adjustment, have at least one year of physical presence and be physically present on filing, satisfy the remaining admissibility and qualified waiver rules, and pay the prescribed fee. The baseline's admission-record date and no-visa-offset rules remain. Extending the parole window is not a new universal parole power, automatic permanent residence, or an extension of every person's adjustment filing deadline.

Section 11208(b) changes only the terminal year in the heading of Afghan Allies Protection Act section 602(b)(3)(F), from 2024 to 2025. It does not amend that paragraph's printed operative visa-number limit, employment-period endpoint, Chief-of-Mission application deadline or exhaustion rule. Those are distinct from the heading and retain their own complete captured qualifications; the candidate does not declare a new visa quota or a new application deadline from this heading edit. The same outer section's Israel loan-guarantee and stockpile amendments are separate fiscal/foreign-assistance context, not personal immigration mechanisms.

Division A sections 1101-1107 would continue the applicable fiscal year 2024 account levels, transfers, obligation limitations, authorities and conditions, subject to the exact listed exceptions and later overrides. DHS division C sections 543-546 are expressly excluded; their old rescissions are not repeated as retained provisions. September 30, 2025 is the default end date, subject to otherwise-provided availability; multi-year and no-year appropriations retain comparable periods. Earlier continuing-resolution expenditures are charged to the applicable funding, not added again. This is not an unrestricted new enforcement authority or permission to restart prohibited activities.

Section 1701(1) sets the ICE operations/support level at $9,986,542,000, replacing the $9,501,542,000 baseline level. The baseline's at least $5,082,218,000 enforcement/detention/removal allocation, including unaccompanied-minor transportation, remains a distinct minimum within a mixed-use account; the account also funds forced-child-labor and intellectual-property enforcement and other specified activities. The complete account total is not assigned solely to removals or detention, and no actual spending or additional sum on top of earlier continuing-resolution expenditures is inferred. CBP operations/support retains the $18,426,870,000 baseline level with its mixed border, customs and other functions. Its $650,000,000 transfer to FEMA for non-Federal sheltering and related activities to relieve CBP short-term holding overcrowding is within that amount, with the $9,100,000 FEMA administrative-cost cap; it is not an extra amount outside the CBP level. USCIS operations/support continues at $271,140,000 for specified operations including E-Verify, refugee/international operations and backlog reduction, additional to other funding without requiring a reduction of the described fees; its $10,000,000 citizenship/integration grant account remains separate.

Section 1706(8) rescinds $2,514,000 of USCIS operations/support unobligated balances made available under the particular section 505 carryover authority. That baseline authority concerns at most 50 percent of fiscal year 2024 operations/support unobligated balances, recorded at notification no later than June 30, 2025, retaining their account/purpose through September 30, 2025 and requiring section 503 notification before obligation. The rescission is not a repeal of all current USCIS funding or fee revenue. Printed fiscal-year and notification language is retained; no blanket year substitution or adjudication of actual balances, notifications or spending is made. Section 1705 removes section 227's force for fiscal year 2025; section 227 is a towing-vessel inspection-fee funding restriction with its own conditions, not an immigration detention safeguard. No actual vessel fee or fee liability is adjudicated.

Retained section 207 bars a defined new universal pedestrian/cyclist/private-vehicle border-crossing fee at northern or southern land ports and studies of imposing it; it does not abolish every existing border-related fee. Under section 212, ICE operations/support funds cannot continue a section 287(g) delegation after the DHS Inspector General determines the governing agreement was materially violated. The complete 1357(g) baseline keeps qualified written state/local agreements, training and federal direction/supervision, specified powers and duration, voluntary participation and separate communication/cooperation savings; no agreement violation or local actor's liability is inferred. Section 213 restricts those same ICE account funds for continuation of detention contracts when both of the two most recent overall facility evaluations are below adequate or its subsequent-system equivalent median score; those evaluations are conducted by ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, not the Inspector General. Neither provision establishes that any particular agreement or facility fails its condition.

Retained sections 527-529 constrain use of the covered DHS funds: congressional oversight access cannot be obstructed or staged by temporary changes, Members need no prior notice, and designated staff may be required to request access 24 hours ahead. The restraint funding bar covers a woman who is pregnant or in post-delivery recuperation. The printed subsection (b) exceptions are phrased for a pregnant woman: an individualized serious-flight-risk or immediate-serious-harm determination where other means cannot prevent the risk, or a medical professional responsible for her care determining therapeutic restraints appropriate for her medical safety. When a pregnant woman is restrained under those exceptions, only the safest and least restrictive restraints determined by the appropriate treating medical professional may be used. Active labor or delivery is an absolute restraint bar; specified positions and constricting restraints are prohibited, with left-side positioning to the maximum feasible extent. Custody death, potential sexual assault/abuse and specified misconduct-allegation records cannot be destroyed with the covered funds; disclosure to a person charged, segregated or otherwise punished for such an allegation requires that person's request and the applicable law, regulations and litigation disclosure rules. These are funding restrictions with retained qualifications, not findings that mistreatment occurred or unconditional disclosure rights.

Retained section 538 requires bimonthly southwest-border arrival estimates covering the current and following fiscal years, with single-adult/family-unit/unaccompanied-child breakdowns, independent validation/verification, interagency sharing and specified planning/budget uses. If the required estimates are not provided for the described purposes, section 503 reprogramming/transfer authority is suspended until the required estimates reach the appropriations committees. Section 540 requires an alternatives and cost-benefit analysis before DHS requests Defense border-security support, a report within 30 days of the request, and another within 30 days after support is granted with quarterly reports during assistance. These requirements do not establish actual arrivals, agency noncompliance, a deployment, or an independently voted preference for military border assistance.

The DHS incorporation in section 1101(a)(6) expressly includes 2024 division G sections 102-105. Their complete printed clauses and material statutory baselines are separately bound. Section 1105's general continuance and section 1106's default September 30, 2025 endpoint are also preserved. The application of that continuance to the incorporated provisions' own September 30, 2024 substitutions and fiscal-year-2024 H-2B conditions is separately reserved for source-grounded review; this candidate neither silently changes their dates nor declares those authorities ineffective solely from the old printed year.

Incorporated section 102 applies a September 30, 2024 substitution to technical-corrections section 220(c), whose applicability sentence concerns persons admitted in J exchange-visitor status or acquiring that status after admission before the specified date. This is not a universal deadline for every physician-waiver application. Complete 1182(e) and 1184(l) retain the qualified two-year foreign-residence waiver framework: favorable recommendation and public-interest finding, the applicable interested agency request and contractual-country no-objection condition, a state-request maximum of 30 per fiscal year, full-time employment with a 90-day start and at least three-year service conditions, shortage-area/specialty requirements with their Veterans Affairs, medical-research/training and up-to-ten state facility exceptions. The qualified change to H-1B status has its own numerical-limit exception; failure to fulfill the contract or continuing public-interest/service conditions retains the stated foreign-residence consequences. No particular physician qualifies or receives a waiver from this incorporation alone.

Incorporated section 103 substitutes the printed September 30, 2024 date in IIRIRA section 401(b)'s program-termination clause. It does not create a universal mandatory E-Verify requirement. The complete 401-405 baseline keeps generally voluntary participation with specific federal-government, legislative-branch and qualifying-violation-order exceptions. Identity/employment confirmation has its own inquiry and secondary-verification process: a tentative nonconfirmation may be contested and is not treated as a final finding of unauthorized employment. Employment cannot be terminated because of failed confirmation until nonconfirmation becomes final, without barring termination for another reason. Continued employment after final nonconfirmation has distinct notification and rebuttable-presumption rules; the candidate does not infer actual ineligibility, mandatory dismissal of every person, system accuracy or employer liability.

Incorporated section 104 applies the printed September 30, 2024 substitution to both non-minister paths in 1101(a)(27)(C)(ii)(II) and (III). The separate minister path in (I) is not given a new date by borrowing the non-minister clauses. The complete definition retains two years of qualifying denomination membership immediately before application, the bona fide nonprofit organization and requested professional/religious-vocation or occupation conditions, continuous prior qualifying work, and the qualified accompanying/following spouse-and-child relationship. It is not permission for every religious worker or a change to every special-immigrant quota.

Incorporated section 105 permits, rather than mandates, a supplemental H-2B increase after DHS consultation with Labor and a determination that the printed fiscal-year-2024 United States business needs cannot be met by willing, qualified and able United States workers for temporary nonagricultural labor. Its increase is bounded by the highest number of H-2B returning-worker-program participants in any fiscal year when those workers were exempt, not an unlimited allotment or an automatic exemption for every returning worker. Complete 1184(g) separately retains the ordinary 66,000 principal-worker annual cap, spouse/child distinction, petition-order and other conditional rules, and the 33,000 first-six-month limit; no precise supplemental count, actual discretionary increase or resolved FY2025 application is inferred. Complete 1101(H) retains the temporary nonagricultural category's foreign-residence, labor-availability and medical-graduate exclusion conditions. This remains a whole-package House passage choice, not a separate vote for any program, employer or applicant.

The retained DHS reporting clauses are distinct obligations with different actors and subjects. Section 215 continues semimonthly public detention reporting through complete 2021 section 216 and 2020 section 218. The ICE Director's report must be downloadable, searchable and sortable, with at least the preceding twelve months of semimonthly data. The continued fields include detention population and book-ins; lengths of stay, transfers, stated fear determinations and notices to appear; alternatives-to-detention enrollment and supervision; facility information, classification/threat/criminality data, inspection results and guaranteed capacity; and releases and removals. The stated single-adult/family and facility disaggregations remain. These are reporting requirements, not observed counts, a new credible-fear decision rule or permission to classify an individual from the report alone.

Complete 2021 section 216 also retains the reporting-period-end average stay for people still detained, including its stated post-determination subset, and the printed detention-duration bins: over two years, over one year to two years, over six months to one year, and less than six months. The candidate preserves those exact endpoints rather than filling unstated boundary cases. Its additional field literally concerns the number of individuals described in 28 CFR 115.5, including use and duration of solitary confinement. Complete historical 115.5 defines numerous custody, staff, facility and gender terms; the appropriation does not name a selected definition. The reporting cohort is separately reserved for source-grounded application review. This candidate selects neither only transgender/intersex people nor every person mentioned in that regulation, and it does not extend all of part 115 through a single definitions reference. Semimonthly is retained; no biweekly schedule or new seven-day initial deadline is inferred from the older baseline.

Section 216 separately reapplies complete 2020 section 217. That agreement report is submitted by the ICE Director, not the Inspector General, to the appropriations committees and posted publicly. Its enumerated fields are participating jurisdictions' community outreach, individuals placed in removal proceedings, state/local officer performance including nationality and criminality, and future agreement-expansion plans. There is no enumerated training-report requirement. The retained report's own 45-day timing is preserved alongside general continuance without assigning an unsupported new deadline. Current section 217 is a different 45-day obligation plan submitted by the ICE Chief Financial Officer, delineated by level II program, project and activity. Neither report is the Inspector General's material-agreement-violation trigger. No actual agreement outcome, violation, report delivery, facility condition or solitary-confinement use is asserted.

The retained CBP procurement controls remain qualified by their own funding scope. Section 208 requires the Commissioner to provide an expenditure plan for current and prior procurement/construction/improvement amounts within its printed 90-day period, and bars obligation of the current Act's covered amounts before that plan. Section 209 applies the complete 2021 fencing restriction to funds made available in this Act: Santa Ana Wildlife Refuge, Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, La Lomita Historical park, the National Butterfly Center, within or east of the Vista del Mar Ranch tract, and historic cemeteries. It is not a prohibition on every border project or every other funding stream. Section 210 permits alteration of National Targeting Center operations but bars reductions of anticipated or planned vetting at existing locations using the specified current, prior-available and fee funds unless specifically authorized by a later statute. No actual project, plan submission or vetting reduction is inferred.

Section 211 earmarks $850,170,000 within the CBP procurement account across separate purposes: $283,500,000 for border-security technologies, $380,900,000 for trade/travel assets and infrastructure, $92,114,000 for facility construction/improvements, $75,983,000 for integrated-operations assets/infrastructure, and $17,673,000 for mission support/infrastructure. This mixed allocation is not an all-wall-construction amount or a claim of actual expenditure. General continuance and the exact printed fiscal-year and availability qualifications remain; no blanket year substitution is performed.

Section 214 permits reprogramming within and transfers to ICE operations/support as necessary for detention of people prioritized for removal, without the time and condition limitation of section 503(d). This is a specific subsection exception, not removal of all transfer caps, advance notices, appropriations conditions or custody safeguards. Complete section 503 separately retains its ordinary reprogramming notification thresholds, transfer caps and exceptions. Its subsection (f) permits up to $20,000,000 to the Immigration Emergency Fund notwithstanding subsection (c), with at least five days' advance appropriations-committee notice. The complete fund baseline authorizes appropriations sufficient for a $35,000,000 balance; it does not establish that balance or actual transfers. General emergency withdrawals require the stated Presidential determination and certification. Paragraph (2) separately permits application-based state/local reimbursement for qualifying requested assistance under its asylum-increase, resident-endangerment or other Attorney General circumstances, with a $20,000,000 aggregate locality cap and a 15-day application-decision rule. That paragraph expressly does not require the paragraph (1) immigration-emergency determination. The transfer ceiling and the separate reimbursement ceiling are not combined into an automatic $40,000,000 allotment; no emergency, reimbursement entitlement or payment is found.

The complete fee-account baseline qualifies the already-bound USCIS additional-funding provision. Section 1356(m) permits fee levels to recover adjudication/naturalization service costs, including similar no-charge asylum or other immigrant services and fee-administration costs; it retains the Virgin Islands and Guam payment provisions. Section 1356(n) keeps deposits available until expended for the described reimbursement of service and fee-administration appropriations. The continuing USCIS appropriation does not require fee reductions; neither that saving nor this baseline fixes a new applicant fee, abolishes fees, converts the account to expiring annual funds or establishes an actual charge.

Retained section 403 permits covered USCIS Federal funds to collect and use biometrics taken at a USCIS Application Support Center overseen virtually by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology. The location and supervision conditions remain. It is not permission for unrestricted home collection, a universal remote-biometric mandate, or a determination of any applicant's eligibility. These remain components of one House package passage choice.

Retained section 512 bars using funds made available in this Act to amend the naturalization oath in INA section 337 (8 USC 1448). It is a funding restriction on amendment, not a new oath, an applicant's eligibility determination or removal of the existing oath's accommodations. The complete baseline retains the qualified religious-training-and-belief accommodations for bearing arms or military service, the child-understanding waiver in its specified naturalization route, and the waiver for inability to understand or communicate understanding because of physical/developmental disability or mental impairment. Their stated showings and official determinations remain; the candidate does not grant a waiver to any person. Public ceremony, title-renunciation and qualified expedited-administration rules remain distinct.

Retained section 514 bars the current Act's funds for planning, testing, piloting or developing a national identification card. It does not abolish all existing identification documents, prohibit every identification-related activity using other funds or establish any person's documentary requirements. Retained section 517 separately bars using the current Act's funds to employ workers described in INA section 274A(h)(3). That definition is employment-specific at the particular time: the person is neither lawfully admitted for permanent residence nor otherwise authorized for that employment under the Act or by the stated authority. This is not a bar on employing every noncitizen, every visa holder or every asylum applicant. No person's actual authorization, employment violation, fee or naturalization outcome is inferred from these package provisions.

No actual admission, adjustment, expenditure, enactment or preferred alternative is inferred.

The 599D(b)(3) one-thousand allocation is within the larger former-Soviet/Baltic-national refugee admissions allocation under 207(a)(3), for the narrower 599D(b)(2)(B) recipient category: are or were nationals of those countries, current Ukrainian Catholic or Ukrainian Orthodox Church members, with public, active and continuous participation (or attempted participation) in that church's religious activities. It is not an additional overall refugee quota or admission for every national or church member.

All three 599D(e) branches are distinct: applications, written denial decisions and reapplications. Before October 1, 2025 is retained literally; there is no claim that every person from a listed country qualifies or is admitted.

Section 11208(b) changes only the Afghan F heading. Unchanged operative limits and deadlines are source-bound separately; no new quota, employment-period extension or application-deadline extension is inferred from the heading.

March 15 enacted Public Law 119-4 is after the March 11 House vote and is not substituted as its governing exact version. The later law already present in the source pool is not a primary meaning binding for this action.

This is the whole package passage choice, not separate support or opposition to any selected provision or individual outcome. Remaining DHS, DOJ, State and other material incorporation work is executable research, not unavailable evidence.

DHS baseline 543-546 are expressly excluded. Section 1705 concerns section 227 towing-vessel inspection fees, not termination of custody safeguards; underlying vessel-fee application remains outside this candidate.

Congressional staff access, pregnancy restraints and custody-record disclosure retain their distinct qualifications. No actual access, violation, abuse, liability or universal disclosure entitlement is inferred.
Border estimates and pre-request Defense-support analyses are retained reporting/control requirements; no forecast, causality, deployment or actual suspension of transfer authority is asserted.

E-Verify participation is generally voluntary with specific statutory exceptions; tentative and final nonconfirmation, contest and termination/notification rules remain distinct. No universal participation mandate or individual unauthorized-employment conclusion.

H2B supplemental authority is discretionary and condition-bound, with a historical returning-worker ceiling formula; it is not a fixed or unlimited new visa quota, universal returning-worker exemption or resolved FY2025 allocation.

The public detention-report chain, retained ICE Director 287(g) agreement report and current ICE Chief Financial Officer obligation plan are separate. No Inspector General reporter or enumerated training field is introduced.

Semimonthly reporting, twelve months of historical data and printed stay-duration endpoints are preserved. No observed counts, repaired boundary bins, biweekly schedule or reset initial report deadline is inferred.

Fencing incorporation concerns the current Act funds and six specified locations, including within or east of Vista del Mar; procurement totals retain their mixed allocations. No actual project, all-funding fence ban or all-wall total.

The biometric permission concerns an Application Support Center virtually overseen by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology, not unrestricted home collection or a universal mandate.

The oath clause bars use of current Act funds to amend the oath; existing qualified religious/child/disability accommodations and ceremony rules remain. No new oath or individual waiver/eligibility decision.
