Senate 100051(8) and (11) are purposes within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. Neither purpose is a separate earmark for the full account, the ICE account or a House child appropriation. Paragraph (8) funds removal operations for specified unaccompanied alien children, but amounts under this paragraph shall only be used for permitting a specified unaccompanied alien child to withdraw the application for admission of the child pursuant to section 235(a)(4). The Secretary of Homeland Security must determine on a case-by-case basis all three specified-child conditions. First, the child has been found by an immigration officer at a land border or port of entry of the United States and is inadmissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Second, the child has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return of the child to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence. Third, the child does not have a fear of returning to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence owing to a credible fear of persecution. The paragraph does not print the House express contiguous-or-non-contiguous-country phrase or an independent-decision finding; neither is silently inserted into its definition. The incorporated unaccompanied-alien-child definition requires no lawful immigration status in the United States and not having attained 18 years of age, together with either no parent or legal guardian in the United States or no parent or legal guardian in the United States available to provide care and physical custody. The complete severe-forms-of-trafficking definition is bound with its own sex-trafficking and labor-or-services alternatives, force/fraud/coercion and under-18 distinctions; no label alone determines a child's eligibility. Paragraph (11) funds criminal and gang checks of defined unaccompanied alien children who are 12 years of age and older, including the examination of such unaccompanied alien children for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings. It prints no separate encountered-by-CBP condition; the House 70116 encounter condition is not imported. Its age-12 floor belongs to this check purpose, not the paragraph (8) withdrawal definition. Examination funding is not a finding that a child belongs to a gang, has committed a crime or is dangerous. Complete material captured pre-vote 235(a)(4) retains discretionary permission to withdraw and depart immediately, not a mandatory withdrawal or removal order. Complete TVPRA 235/1232 retains its own contiguous-child case-by-case trafficking/fear and independent-decision conditions, discretionary withdrawal/return, safe-return conditions, 48-hour screening and failed-or-undetermined-screen transfer, other-child custody pathway and own notification/72-hour-transfer exceptions. Its removal-proceedings, relief/access-to-counsel, placement, suitability and remaining safeguards retain their own scope. Senate funding does not itself establish their repeal, fulfillment or a universal individual return, protection or counsel outcome. Exact application interaction remains separate question 49; House question 43 is preserved independently.

Senate 100051(5) fingerprint and DNA purposes are within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 Secretary of Homeland Security account through September 30, 2029. Both purposes share the printed circumstance of aliens and alien children entering the United States without a valid visa. Subparagraph (A) funds collecting fingerprints, in accordance with section 262 and subsections (a)(3) and (b) of section 235 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Subparagraph (B) separately funds collecting DNA, in accordance with sections 235(d) and 287(b) of that Act. These are funding purposes with their own incorporated authorities, not a determination that every alien or child is subject to every collection power or that funded collection actually occurred. Captured 262(a) concerns an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is fourteen years of age or older, has not been registered and fingerprinted under section 1201(b) or section 30 or 31 of the Alien Registration Act, 1940, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer. All those conditions are common to its duty to apply for registration and to be fingerprinted before the expiration of such thirty days. Captured 262(b) separately requires a parent or legal guardian to apply for registration of an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is less than fourteen years of age, has not been registered under those named provisions, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer, before that period expires. That parent/guardian provision prints registration, not the same under-14 fingerprint duty. Whenever an alien attains his fourteenth birthday in the United States, the separate rule requires in-person registration and fingerprinting within thirty days thereafter. Captured 262(c) retains the Attorney General's discretionary nonimmigrant fingerprint waiver on the basis of reciprocity pursuant to prescribed regulations; no actual waiver is inferred. Complete 235(a)(3) concerns inspection of aliens, including crewmen, who apply for or otherwise seek admission, readmission or transit; it does not itself print a fingerprint command. Complete material 235(b)(1)/(2) screening, exceptions, asylum/fear/interview/review/consultation/detention and contiguous-return conditions remain bound, together with the original favorable-admission challenge. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 renumbers that original challenge from (3) to (4) and inserts the distinct State enforcement (3); the captured 2024 wording is not relabeled as an unamended 2025 subsection. Complete 235(d) retains its own belief-based conveyance search, detention/delivery with the alien-crewmember exception, named oath/evidence powers and subpoena-purpose/court-enforcement conditions. Complete 287(b) retains the designated officer/employee oath/evidence scope and its own knowing-or-willful false-evidence/perjury conditions. Neither cited provision expressly names DNA collection. That literal observation does not resolve whether other law, implementation rules or this funding language supports a proposed collection; question 50 reserves the exact DNA authority/application interaction. Question 51 separately reserves the fingerprint-purpose no-valid-visa circumstance alongside the incorporated registration age/prior-registration/duration/waiver paths and inspection procedures. No statutory repeal, guaranteed discretion outcome, universal biometric collection or actual child/parent/status/registration finding is inferred.

Remaining Senate 100051 purposes (1) through (4), (6), (7) and (12) share the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. They are purposes within that account, not separate full-envelope earmarks or borrowed ICE/House amounts. The paragraph 1 purpose is hiring and training of additional U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents, and the necessary support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities. The paragraph 2 purpose is funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with the departure or removal of aliens. The paragraph 3 purpose is funding for the assignment of Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement activities pursuant to sections 103(a) and 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 1357(g)). The paragraph 4 purpose is hiring additional staff and investing the necessary resources to enhance screening and vetting of all aliens seeking entry into United States, consistent with section 212 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1182), or intending to remain in the United States, consistent with section 237 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1227). The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting and facilitating the return, pursuant to section 235(b)(2)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(C)), of aliens arriving from contiguous territory. The paragraph 7 purpose is funding for State and local participation in homeland security efforts for purposes of: ending the presence of criminal gangs and criminal organizations throughout the United States; addressing crime and public safety threats; combating human smuggling and trafficking networks throughout the United States; supporting immigration enforcement activities; and providing reimbursement for State and local participation in such efforts. The paragraph 12 purpose is information technology investments to support immigration purposes, including improvements to fee and revenue collections. The entry and intended-remain screening categories retain their own section 212 and section 237 references. The State/local participation list retains all five own purposes, including its own throughout-the-United-States phrases. It does not borrow the reimbursement fund's crime-plus-unlawful-presence category or domestic transport restriction. The general departure/removal transportation purpose prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase. The assignment list retains Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers pursuant to both printed statutory references, not authority for any State employee to exercise all Federal powers. The printed purpose lists do not determine that a particular expenditure must fulfill every listed category. Fee and revenue collection IT is not a new fee, fine or penalty charge. Complete captured 103(a) retains its named agency roles, regulatory/delegation powers, consents and other conditions. In captured 103(a)(10), the Attorney General may authorize a State or local law enforcement officer to perform or exercise any of the powers, privileges, or duties conferred or imposed by this chapter or regulations issued thereunder upon officers or employees of the Service only in the event of the Attorney General's determination that an actual or imminent mass influx of aliens arriving off the coast of the United States, or near a land border, presents urgent circumstances requiring an immediate Federal response, and with the consent of the head of the department, agency, or establishment under whose jurisdiction the individual is serving. The captured event-specific authorization does not establish general unconditioned State power. Previously bound full 287(g) agreement qualifications, training, written powers/duration, Federal direction/supervision, voluntary/communication/cooperation and expense/employment/liability distinctions remain unchanged. Complete captured section 212(a) grounds and remaining operative section 212 authorities retain their own standards, exceptions, discretionary waivers and conditional notice rules, not an every-alien crime finding or guaranteed notice/waiver. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 replaces the original Attorney General references in 212(d)(5) with Secretary of Homeland Security and adds the distinct State enforcement route. Original captured 2024 words are preserved with that amending law, not relabeled as the complete unamended 2025 section. Complete captured section 237 retains distinct deportability grounds, actual conviction/knowledge/timing or other own requirements, exceptions/waivers, special nonimmigrant and SIJ boundaries and conditional administrative stays; screening funding does not determine an individual inadmissible, deportable or criminal. The contiguous-return purpose is pursuant to 235(b)(2)(C). The captured 235(b)(2)(C) return authority concerns an applicant for admission whom the examining immigration officer determines is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, arriving on land (whether or not at a designated port of arrival) from a foreign territory contiguous to the United States. The Attorney General may return that alien to that territory pending a proceeding under section 1229a. The captured parent exceptions for a crewman, an alien to whom paragraph (1) applies, and a stowaway remain. Discretionary return is not a final removal order or universal cross-border return duty. Complete captured 240 proceedings retain judge/charge/exclusive-procedure exceptions, own representation and evidence/examination limits, burdens, decision/appeal, motion and notice/deadline/stay rules. No guaranteed relief, government-paid counsel or individual hearing/return result is inferred. Other H.R.1 immigration components and separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

The Senate 90005(b) State Border Security Reinforcement Fund is a distinct DHS fund. Its complete selected operative clauses are retained below. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 1: There is established, in the Department of Homeland Security, a fund to be known as the ``State Border Security Reinforcement Fund.'' Senate 90005(b) paragraph 2: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts appropriated or otherwise made available for the Fund for grants to eligible States and units of local government for any of the following purposes: Senate 90005(b) purpose A: Construction or installation of a border wall, border fencing or other barrier, or buoys along the southern border of the United States, which may include planning, procurement of materials, and personnel costs related to such construction or installation. Senate 90005(b) purpose B: Any work necessary to prepare the ground at or near land borders to allow construction and maintenance of a border wall or other barrier fencing. Senate 90005(b) purpose C: Detection and interdiction of illicit substances and aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States and have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, and transfer or referral of such aliens to the Department of Homeland Security as provided by law. Senate 90005(b) purpose D: Relocation of aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States from small population centers to other domestic locations. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 3: In addition to amounts otherwise available for the purposes described in paragraph (2), there is appropriated for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to the Department of Homeland Security for the State Border Security Reinforcement Fund established by paragraph (1), $10,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2034, for qualified expenses for such purposes. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 4: The Secretary of Homeland Security may provide grants from the fund established by paragraph (1) to State agencies and units of local governments for expenditures made for completed, ongoing, or new activities, in accordance with law, that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 5: Each State desiring to apply for a grant under this subsection shall submit an application to the Secretary containing such information in support of the application as the Secretary may require. The Secretary shall require that each State include in its application the purposes for which the State seeks the funds and a description of how the State plans to allocate the funds. The Secretary shall begin to accept applications not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 6: Nothing in this subsection shall authorize any State or local government to exercise immigration or border security authorities reserved exclusively to the Federal Government under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) or the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). The Federal Emergency Management Agency may use not more than 1 percent of the funds made available under this subsection for the purpose of administering grants provided for in this section. The paragraph (2)(C) alien category retains both unlawful entry and commission of a crime under Federal, State, or local law; those alien predicates do not classify illicit substances. Transfer or referral remains as provided by law. Paragraph (2)(D) instead concerns unlawful presence and relocation from small population centers to other domestic locations; it does not borrow the crime or unlawful-entry predicates from (C), or authorize an international return. Only (A) specifies the southern border; (B) says at or near land borders. The paragraph (2) eligible-State/local-unit grant purpose rule and paragraph (4) discretionary State-agency/local-government expenditure rule remain distinct. The paragraph (5) application obligations name each State; no additional local-government obligation is inferred. The 90-day clause concerns when the Secretary must begin accepting applications, not an applicant deadline or a finding that applications are open. The paragraph (6) construction rule preserves exclusively Federal authorities without deciding which actual functions or expenditures fall within that reservation. The FEMA administration ceiling is discretionary, no more than 1 percent of funds under this subsection for grants in this section; its two scope words remain distinct. This is not an actual award, expenditure, eligibility, individual status/crime, relocation, power delegation or reimbursement determination. House reimbursement amounts, availability, January 21 date and duplicate-reimbursement restriction are not imported. Other package components and the 51 separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected Senate 90005(a) funding and its own program context follow. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 1: In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to be administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program authorized under section 2004 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605), to enhance State, local, and Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and other activities-- Senate 90005(a) purpose A: $500,000,000 for State and local capabilities to detect, identify, track, or monitor threats from unmanned aircraft systems (as such term is defined in section 44801 of title 49, United States Code), consistent with titles 18 and 49 of the United States Code; Senate 90005(a) purpose B: $625,000,000 for security and other costs related to the 2026 FIFA World Cup; Senate 90005(a) purpose C: $1,000,000,000 for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2028 Olympics; and Senate 90005(a) purpose D: $450,000,000 for the Operation Stonegarden Grant Program. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 2: None of the funds made available under subparagraph (B) or (C) of paragraph (1) shall be subject to the requirements of section 2004(e)(1) or section 2008(a)(12) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605(e)(1), 609(a)(12)). The pre-vote fiscal year 2024 DHS/FEMA HSGP notice reproduced on Hawaii's official host describes Operation Stonegarden as supporting enhanced cooperation and coordination among CBP, USBP, and Federal, State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to improve overall border security. It funds joint border-security efforts along routes of ingress and egress to and from international borders, including travel corridors in States bordering Mexico and Canada and States and territories with international water borders. In that notice, those State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies use their inherent law enforcement authorities and receive no additional authority from participating in Stonegarden. This is dated program-purpose context, not a new power conferred by the Senate appropriation or a complete 2025 eligibility rule. The additional fiscal year 2025 appropriation names FEMA Administrator, availability until September 30, 2029, administration under the State Homeland Security Grant Program in 6 U.S.C. 605, and State/local/Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements and other activities. The Stonegarden purpose is $450,000,000 within that administration provision. The drone-threat, FIFA and Olympics purposes retain their own printed objects and amounts as adjacent context; those purposes alone do not establish an immigration purpose. The exemption from 605(e)(1) minimum allocation and 609(a)(12) grant-administration expense cap expressly names only FIFA paragraph (1)(B) and Olympics paragraph (1)(C); no exemption for Stonegarden paragraph (1)(D) or drone paragraph (1)(A) is inferred. Captured 605(e)(1) retains its State and named-territory minimum-allocation branches, own fiscal-year denominators and percentages; captured 609(a)(12) permits expenses directly related to grant administration except that such expenses may not exceed 3 percent of the grant amount. Neither this cap nor those minima are reclassified as the separate 90005(b) FEMA one-percent ceiling. Complete captured 603, 605 and 609 retain their own program relationships, application/distribution/multistate rules, permitted-use and personnel/construction/recreation restrictions, waivers, reimbursement, transfers and equipment requirements. Their application to a particular 2025 Stonegarden award, including interaction with the dated 2024 notice's separate HSGP components and conditions, is reserved as question 52. No 2024 funding amount, application deadline, performance period, subrecipient tier or approval automatically governs this new appropriation. Selected exact Senate 70119 death/disability loan-discharge income-exclusion and SSN provisions follow. Senate 70119 exclusion grounds: In the case of an individual, gross income does not include any amount which (but for this subsection) would be includible in gross income for such taxable year by reason of the discharge (in whole or in part) of any loan described in subparagraph (B), if such discharge was-- (i) pursuant to subsection (a) or (d) of section 437 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 or the parallel benefit under part D of title IV of such Act (relating to the repayment of loan liability), (ii) pursuant to section 464(c)(1)(F) of such Act, or (iii) otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. Senate 70119 loan categories: A loan is described in this subparagraph if such loan is-- (i) a student loan (as defined in paragraph (2)), or (ii) a private education loan (as defined in section 140(a) of the Consumer Credit Protection Act (15 U.S.C. 1650(a)). Senate 70119 identification and own marital rules: (i) In general.--Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any discharge during any taxable year unless the taxpayer includes the taxpayer's social security number on the return of tax for such taxable year. (ii) Social security number.--For purposes of this subparagraph, the term `social security number' has the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7).. Senate 70119 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by this Act, is further amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (V), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (W) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (W) the following new subparagraph: (X) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 108(f)(5)(C) (relating to discharges on account of death or disability).. Senate 70119 discharge-date applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to discharges after December 31, 2025. Each version replaces only 108(f)(5) with the printed exclusion, not all of section 108 or every student-loan tax rule. The original 2024 (5) instead covers its defined discharge categories after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2026; the candidate does not silently extend that entire temporary rule unchanged. The common requirement that the discharged loan meet new subparagraph (B) applies across all three ground alternatives. Interaction of that gate, complete loan definitions and the parent-borrower 437(d) reference is reserved as question 55; no blanket conclusion that every HEA discharge qualifies for tax exclusion. Original (f)(1) service-conditioned discharge and (4) named repayment-program exclusions remain separate. New loan categories retain full 108(f)(2) student-loan definition and entire 140(a) private-education definitions, including actual (a)(8) private loan, own private-lender and expense meanings and excluded credit/mortgage categories. This does not mean every education-related debt qualifies. The three exclusion-ground alternatives remain separate: the first two use their specified HEA discharge paths, while only the third prints otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. A parent borrower is not silently equated to the student. Full 437(a) retains qualifying loans, death/disability determinations, safeguards, conditional reinstatement, VA documentation and own income-monitoring/approval/opt-out/update rules; 437(d) separately addresses a parent loan when the student dies. Captured 464(c)(1)(F) retains loan-fund agreement scope, borrower death, regulated permanent/total disability, the medically determinable substantial-gainful-activity alternative with its own duration/death tests, and VA unemployability due to service-connected disability. Part D parallel benefit is retained with complete captured 455 and its unless-otherwise-specified limitation, not a universal cancellation promise. Tax exclusion after a qualifying discharge is distinct from authority to cancel a loan. Both versions define the SSN by 24(h)(7), with their own same-bill amended definition and previously bound SSA issuance authority: citizen or the specified authorization route, and issuance before the return due date, not a bare identification number or a citizen-only rule. No child-credit amount or qualifying-child requirement is imported into the loan exclusion. Math-error treatment retains the existing notice and conditional abatement/deficiency procedure, including the 60-day abatement-request path; it is not a fraud finding or actual assessment. The effective date is discharges after December 31, 2025, not taxable years beginning after that date. No individual exclusion, discharge, marital status, SSA-number validity or return result is inferred. Senate requires the taxpayer SSN on the return and does not print the House conditional-spouse requirement or similar-32(d) addition. Those House clauses are not borrowed. Senate further amends the as-amended math-error list by adding (X), not House (W). House application question 54 is not treated as a settled Senate marital rule. Other H.R.1 components and all separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected exact Senate account and separate pilot eligibility clauses follow. Senate 70204 IRA treatment with own exceptions: Except as provided in this section or under regulations or guidance established by the Secretary, a Trump account shall be treated for purposes of this title in the same manner as an individual retirement account under section 408(a). Senate 70204 account establishment and instrument: The term `Trump account' means an individual retirement account (as defined in section 408(a)) which is not designated as a Roth IRA and which meets the following requirements: (A) The account-- (i) is created or organized by the Secretary for the exclusive benefit of an eligible individual or such eligible individual's beneficiaries, or (ii) is-- (I) created or organized in the United States for the exclusive benefit of an individual who has not attained the age of 18 before the end of the calendar year, or such individual's beneficiaries, and (II) funded by a qualified rollover contribution. (B) The account is designated (in such manner as the Secretary shall prescribe) at the time of the establishment of the account as a Trump account. (C) The written governing instrument creating the account meets the following requirements: (i) No contribution will be accepted-- (I) before the date that is 12 months after the date of the enactment of this section, or (II) in the case of a contribution made in any calendar year before the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18, if such contribution would result in aggregate contributions (other than exempt contributions) for such calendar year in excess of the contribution limit specified in subsection (c)(2)(A). (ii) Except as provided in subsection (d), no distribution will be allowed before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18. (iii) No part of the account funds will be invested in any asset other than an eligible investment during any period before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18. Senate 70204 eligible individual and reciprocal election paths: The term `eligible individual' means any individual-- (A) who has not attained the age of 18 before the close of the calendar year in which the election under subparagraph (C) is made, (B) for whom a social security number (within the meaning of section 24(h)(7)) has been issued before the date on which an election under subsection (C) is made, and (C) for whom-- (i) an election is made under this subparagraph by the Secretary if the Secretary determines (based on information available to the Secretary from tax returns or otherwise) that such individual meets the requirements of subparagraphs (A) and (B) and no prior election has been made for such individual under clause (ii), or (ii) an election is made under this subparagraph by a person other than the Secretary (at such time and in such manner as the Secretary may prescribe) for the establishment of a Trump account if no prior election has been made for such individual under clause (i). Senate 70204 account beneficiary: The term `account beneficiary' means the individual on whose behalf the Trump account was established. Senate 70204 full-balance account rollover: For purposes of this section, the term `qualified rollover contribution' means an amount which is paid in a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer from a Trump account maintained for the benefit of the account beneficiary to a Trump account maintained for such beneficiary, but only if the amount of such payment is equal to the entire balance of the Trump account from which the payment is made. Senate 70204 elected child payment: In the case of an individual who makes an election under this section with respect to an eligible child of the individual, such eligible child shall be treated as making a payment against the tax imposed by subtitle A (for the taxable year for which the election was made) in an amount equal to $1,000. Senate 70204 refund to child account: The amount treated as a payment under subsection (a) shall be paid by the Secretary to the Trump account with respect to which such eligible child is the account beneficiary. Senate 70204 pilot birth window, no prior election and citizenship: For purposes of this section, the term `eligible child' means a qualifying child (as defined in section 152(c))-- (1) who is born after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029, (2) with respect to whom no prior election has been made under this section by such individual or any other individual, and (3) who is a United States citizen. Senate 70204 pilot election administration: An election under this section shall be made at such time and in such manner as the Secretary shall provide. Senate 70204 pilot child identification and election-date definition: (1) In general.--This section shall not apply to any taxpayer unless such individual includes with the election made under this section the social security number of the eligible child with respect to whom the election is made. (2) Social security number defined.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `social security number' shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7), determined by substituting `before the date of the election made under section 6434' for `before the due date of such return' in subparagraph (B) thereof. Senate 70204 payment offset exception: Any payment made to any individual under this section shall not be-- (1) subject to reduction or offset pursuant to subsection (c), (d), (e), or (f) of section 6402 or any similar authority permitting offset, or (2) reduced or offset by other assessed Federal taxes that would otherwise be subject to levy or collection. Senate 70204 payment interest start: The period determined under section 6611(a) with respect to any payment under this section shall not begin before January 1, 2028. Senate 70204 mirror-code election: In the case of any possession of the United States with a mirror code tax system (as defined in section 24(k)), this section shall not be treated as part of the income tax laws of the United States for purposes of determining the income tax law of such possession unless such possession elects to have this section be so treated. Senate 70204 pilot account definitions: For purposes of this section, the terms `Trump account' and `account beneficiary' have the meaning given such terms in section 530A(b).. Senate 70204 improper-election penalty and incorporated definitions: In the case of any individual who makes an election under section 6434 with respect to an individual who is not an eligible child of the taxpayer-- (1) if such election was made due to negligence or disregard of the rules or regulations, there shall be imposed a penalty of $500, or (2) if such election was made due to fraud, there shall be imposed a penalty of $1,000. (b) Definitions.-- (1) Eligible child.--The term `eligible child' has the meaning given such term under section 6434. (2) Negligence; disregard.--The terms `negligence' and `disregard' have the same meaning as when such terms are used in section 6662.. Senate 70204 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by the preceding provisions of this Act, is amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (Y), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (Z) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (Z) the following new subparagraph: (AA) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 6434(e)(1) (relating to the Trump accounts contribution pilot program).. Selected exact Senate tips and overtime deduction/identification clauses follow. Senate 70201 deduction and reporting gate: There shall be allowed as a deduction an amount equal to the qualified tips received during the taxable year that are included on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(3), 6041A(e)(3), 6050W(f)(2), or 6051(a)(18), or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (or successor). Senate 70201 amount and income limits: (1) In general.--The amount allowed as a deduction under this section for any taxable year shall not exceed $25,000. (2) Limitation based on adjusted gross income.-- (A) In general.--The amount allowable as a deduction under subsection (a) (after application of paragraph (1)) shall be reduced (but not below zero) by $100 for each $1,000 by which the taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income exceeds $150,000 ($300,000 in the case of a joint return). (B) Modified adjusted gross income.--For purposes of this paragraph, the term `modified adjusted gross income' means the adjusted gross income of the taxpayer for the taxable year increased by any amount excluded from gross income under section 911, 931, or 933. Senate 70201 non-employee business-income limit: In the case of qualified tips received by an individual during any taxable year in the course of a trade or business (other than the trade or business of performing services as an employee) of such individual, such qualified tips shall be taken into account under subsection (a) only to the extent that the gross income for the taxpayer from such trade or business for such taxable year (including such qualified tips) exceeds the sum of the deductions (other than the deduction allowed under this section) allocable to the trade or business in which such qualified tips are received by the individual for such taxable year. Senate 70201 qualified-tip conditions: For purposes of this section-- (1) In general.--The term `qualified tips' means cash tips received by an individual in an occupation which customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, as provided by the Secretary. (2) Exclusions.--Such term shall not include any amount received by an individual unless-- (A) such amount is paid voluntarily without any consequence in the event of nonpayment, is not the subject of negotiation, and is determined by the payor, (B) the trade or business in the course of which the individual receives such amount is not a specified service trade or business (as defined in section 199A(d)(2)), and (C) such other requirements as may be established by the Secretary in regulations or other guidance are satisfied. For purposes of subparagraph (B), in the case of an individual receiving tips in the trade or business of performing services as an employee, such individual shall be treated as receiving tips in the course of a trade or business which is a specified service trade or business if the trade or business of the employer is a specified service trade or business. (3) Cash tips.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `cash tips' includes tips received from customers that are paid in cash or charged and, in the case of an employee, tips received under any tip-sharing arrangement. Senate 70201 identification: (1) In general.--No deduction shall be allowed under this section unless the taxpayer includes on the return of tax for the taxable year such individual's social security number. (2) Social security number defined.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `social security number' shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7). Senate 70201 own married-individual joint-return rule: If the taxpayer is a married individual (within the meaning of section 7703), this section shall apply only if the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year. Senate 70201 anti-reclassification regulations: The Secretary shall prescribe such regulations or other guidance as may be necessary to prevent reclassification of income as qualified tips, including regulations or other guidance to prevent abuse of the deduction allowed by this section. Senate 70201 deduction termination: No deduction shall be allowed under this section for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028.. Senate 70201 non-itemizer deduction: Section 63(b) is amended by striking and at the end of paragraph (3), by striking the period at the end of paragraph (4) and inserting , and, and by adding at the end the following new paragraph: (5) the deduction provided in section 224.. Senate 70201 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by the preceding provisions of this Act, is amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (W), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (X) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (X) the following new subparagraph: (Y) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 224(e) (relating to deduction for qualified tips).. Senate 70201 tax-year applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Senate 70202 deduction and reporting gate: There shall be allowed as a deduction an amount equal to the qualified overtime compensation received during the taxable year and included on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(4) or 6051(a)(19). Senate 70202 amount and income limits: (1) In general.--The amount allowed as a deduction under this section for any taxable year shall not exceed $12,500 ($25,000 in the case of a joint return). (2) Limitation based on adjusted gross income.-- (A) In general.--The amount allowable as a deduction under subsection (a) (after application of paragraph (1)) shall be reduced (but not below zero) by $100 for each $1,000 by which the taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income exceeds $150,000 ($300,000 in the case of a joint return). (B) Modified adjusted gross income.--For purposes of this paragraph, the term `modified adjusted gross income' means the adjusted gross income of the taxpayer for the taxable year increased by any amount excluded from gross income under section 911, 931, or 933. Senate 70202 qualified-overtime conditions: (1) In general.--For purposes of this section, the term `qualified overtime compensation' means overtime compensation paid to an individual required under section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 that is in excess of the regular rate (as used in such section) at which such individual is employed. (2) Exclusions.--Such term shall not include any qualified tip (as defined in section 224(d)). Senate 70202 identification: (1) In general.--No deduction shall be allowed under this section unless the taxpayer includes on the return of tax for the taxable year such individual's social security number. (2) Social security number defined.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `social security number' shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7). Senate 70202 own married-individual joint-return rule: If the taxpayer is a married individual (within the meaning of section 7703), this section shall apply only if the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year. Senate 70202 regulations: The Secretary shall issue such regulations or other guidance as may be necessary or appropriate to carry out the purposes of this section, including regulations or other guidance to prevent abuse of the deduction allowed by this section. Senate 70202 deduction termination: No deduction shall be allowed under this section for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028.. Senate 70202 non-itemizer deduction: Section 63(b), as amended by the preceding provisions of this Act, is amended by striking and at the end of paragraph (4), by striking the period at the end of paragraph (5) and inserting , and, and by adding at the end the following new paragraph: (6) the deduction provided in section 225.. Senate 70202 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by the preceding provisions of this Act, is amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (X), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (Y) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (Y) the following new subparagraph: (Z) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 225(d) (relating to deduction for qualified overtime).. Senate 70202 tax-year applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. These provisions allow deductions for their own qualified income, not exemption of every dollar described colloquially as tips or overtime and not a guarantee of zero tax. Each retains the complete printed qualified-income gates and its own new statutory subsection references; statements/Form 4137 references, business net-income limits, exceptions and regulatory instructions are not omitted. The original 199A(d)(2) service-business definition is bound with its own 1202/475 references, without importing the separate 199A(d)(3) qualified-business-income phase-in as an automatic tips exception or classifying an actual profession. Overtime means compensation required under FLSA section 7 in excess of the regular rate, not all compensation for hours described as overtime or a taxpayer employment determination. Complete original section 7 with common applicability, regular-rate inclusions/exclusions, alternative arrangements, compensatory-time and other own limitations is bound; no universal 40-hour or all-worker eligibility claim is inferred. All four SSN definitions use their own same-bill 24(h)(7) and full SSA issuance route: citizen or specified authorization, issued before the return due date, not every SSN or a citizen-only rule. Neither a valid number nor filing alone establishes the deduction. All four deduction sections apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and deny deductions for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2028; tax-year language is not a discharge/event deadline or repeal of all related reporting/business-credit rules. Other financial/reporting context remains in complete source bindings without an actual implementation conclusion. Other H.R.1 components and separately reserved questions remain unfinished. Senate tips caps deduction at $25,000; overtime at $12,500 or $25,000 for a joint return, each with $100 per $1,000 over $150,000/$300,000 MAGI phaseout and own 911/931/933 additions. Senate tips uses own cash/charged/tip-sharing and employee/employer service-business clauses; overtime excludes qualified tips, without importing House highly-compensated/earned-income exclusions. Senate inserts math-error (Y) for tips and (Z) for overtime. No House spouse, similar-marital, compensation-threshold, extra-quote or distinct qualified-tip subsection rule is borrowed.

Selected exact Senate 20011 DOD border-support funding and authority boundaries follow. Senate 20011 incorporated chapter 15 section 275: The Secretary of Defense shall prescribe such regulations as may be necessary to ensure that any activity (including the provision of any equipment or facility or the assignment or detail of any personnel) under this chapter does not include or permit direct participation by a member of the Army, Navy, Air Force, or Marine Corps in a search, seizure, arrest, or other similar activity unless participation in such activity by such member is otherwise authorized by law. Senate 20011 incorporated chapter 15 section 276: Support (including the provision of any equipment or facility or the assignment or detail of any personnel) may not be provided to any civilian law enforcement official under this chapter if the provision of such support will adversely affect the military preparedness of the United States. The Secretary of Defense shall prescribe such regulations as may be necessary to ensure that the provision of any such support does not adversely affect the military preparedness of the United States. Senate 20011 incorporated chapter 15 section 278: Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to limit the authority of the executive branch in the use of military personnel or equipment for civilian law enforcement purposes beyond that provided by law before December 1, 1981. Senate 20011 chapter 15 counterdrug short-term preparedness waiver: Notwithstanding section 276 of this title, the Secretary may provide support pursuant to subsection (a) in any case in which the Secretary determines that the provision of such support would adversely affect the military preparedness of the United States in the short term if the Secretary determines that the importance of providing such support outweighs such short-term adverse effect. Senate 20011 chapter 15 counterdrug relationship and exceptions: (1) Additional authority .—The authority provided in this section for the support of counterdrug activities or activities to counter transnational organized crime by the Department of Defense is in addition to, and except as provided in paragraph (2), not subject to the other requirements of this chapter. No status/crime/detention-duration/child/family condition is invented from other DHS/ICE grants or from the parent package. Funding a stated activity does not by itself resolve which military/civilian actor may exercise each power or establish a universal arrest/search/detention authorization. Whole original chapter 15 operative sections 271-284 are bound, with civilian-request, applicable-law, jurisdiction, support-type, geography, approval, military-readiness, reimbursement, notice/report and agency/definition conditions. They are not all simultaneously universal duties: 277(b) has its own National Guard support boundary; 282/283 have emergency/DOJ/approval conditions; 284 has its own additional-authority/exception/limited-waiver rules. Section 275 retains regulation duty, named Army/Navy/Air Force/Marine Corps members, direct search/seizure/arrest/similar activity restriction and unless otherwise authorized by law. Section 276 preparedness condition is retained with the actual 284(e) short-term adverse-effect/two-determination waiver and 284(g) relationship; no absolute no-adverse-effect summary or universal waiver. Section 278 preserves prior executive authority rather than granting an unlimited new enforcement power. Full 284 retains authorized requestors, domestic/foreign and 25-mile conditions, drug-corridor construction, notice/reports and definitions; no general migrant-detainment or all-border-construction authority inferred from the chapter heading. Original numerical legacy references in 273/274/279/282/283 remain as printed, without silent repair or interpretation by title alone. Proposed national-defense-area/temporary-detention/direct-participation and support-path application is reserved as question 61, with all relevant lawful-authority conditions, rather than accepted or declared categorically unlawful. Other H.R.1 components and separately reserved questions remain unfinished. Senate appropriates $1 billion and expressly ends its stated funding purposes with in accordance with chapter 15 of title 10. Full incorporated authority and selected complete restriction/exception clauses above qualify the candidate without deciding an actual activity. Selected exact Senate 87001 ORR sponsor-vetting funding and own purpose boundaries follow. Senate 87001 ORR appropriation: (a) Appropriation.--In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Office of Refugee Resettlement for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $300,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2028, for the purposes described in subsection (b). Senate 87001 exclusive funded-purpose boundary: (b) Use of Funds.--The funds made available under subsection (a) may only be used for the Office of Refugee Resettlement to support costs associated with-- Senate 87001 background-check purpose and required contents: (1) background checks on potential sponsors, which shall include-- (A) the name of the potential sponsor and of all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (B) the social security number or tax payer identification number of the potential sponsor and of all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (C) the date of birth of the potential sponsor and of all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (D) the validated location of the residence at which the unaccompanied alien child will be placed; (E) an in-person or virtual interview with, and suitability study concerning, the potential sponsor and all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (F) contact information for the potential sponsor and for all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; and (G) the results of all background and criminal records checks for the potential sponsor and for all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household, which shall include, at a minimum, an investigation of the public records sex offender registry, a public records background check, and a national criminal history check based on fingerprints; Senate 87001 home-study purpose: (2) home studies of potential sponsors of unaccompanied alien children; Senate 87001 child examination and covering purpose: (3) determining whether an unaccompanied alien child poses a danger to self or others by conducting an examination of the unaccompanied alien child for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings and covering such tattoos or markings while the child is in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement; Senate 87001 data-system purpose: (4) data systems improvement and sharing that supports the health, safety, and well being of unaccompanied alien children by determining the appropriateness of potential sponsors of unaccompanied alien children and of adults residing in the household of the potential sponsor and by assisting with the identification and investigation of child labor exploitation and child trafficking; and Senate 87001 State child-welfare coordination purpose: (5) coordinating and communicating with State child welfare agencies regarding the placement of unaccompanied alien children in such States by the Office of Refugee Resettlement. Senate 87001 own sponsor and child definitions: (c) Definitions.--In this section: (1) Potential sponsor.--The term potential sponsor means an individual or entity who applies for the custody of an unaccompanied alien child. (2) Unaccompanied alien child.--The term unaccompanied alien child has the meaning given such term in section 462(g) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 279(g)). Original 279(g) incorporated category boundary: The incorporated unaccompanied alien child category requires all three conditions: has no lawful immigration status in the United States; has not attained 18 years of age; and either there is no parent or legal guardian in the United States, or no parent or legal guardian in the United States is available to provide care and physical custody. Placement means the placement of an unaccompanied alien child in either a detention facility or an alternative to such a facility. Age alone does not establish this category, and availability for care and physical custody is retained. Original 1232(c)(2)-(3) placement and suitability protections: (2) Safe and secure placements (A) Minors in department of health and human services custody Subject to section 279(b)(2) of title 6, an unaccompanied alien child in the custody of the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall be promptly placed in the least restrictive setting that is in the best interest of the child. In making such placements, the Secretary may consider danger to self, danger to the community, and risk of flight. Placement of child trafficking victims may include placement in an Unaccompanied Refugee Minor program, pursuant to section 412(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1522(d)), if a suitable family member is not available to provide care. A child shall not be placed in a secure facility absent a determination that the child poses a danger to self or others or has been charged with having committed a criminal offense. The placement of a child in a secure facility shall be reviewed, at a minimum, on a monthly basis, in accordance with procedures prescribed by the Secretary, to determine if such placement remains warranted. (B) Aliens transferred from Department of Health and Human Services to Department of Homeland Security custody If a minor described in subparagraph (A) reaches 18 years of age and is transferred to the custody of the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Secretary shall consider placement in the least restrictive setting available after taking into account the alien's danger to self, danger to the community, and risk of flight. Such aliens shall be eligible to participate in alternative to detention programs, utilizing a continuum of alternatives based on the alien's need for supervision, which may include placement of the alien with an individual or an organizational sponsor, or in a supervised group home. (3) Safety and suitability assessments (A) In general Subject to the requirements of subparagraph (B), an unaccompanied alien child may not be placed with a person or entity unless the Secretary of Health and Human Services makes a determination that the proposed custodian is capable of providing for the child's physical and mental well-being. Such determination shall, at a minimum, include verification of the custodian's identity and relationship to the child, if any, as well as an independent finding that the individual has not engaged in any activity that would indicate a potential risk to the child. (B) Home studies Before placing the child with an individual, the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall determine whether a home study is first necessary. A home study shall be conducted for a child who is a victim of a severe form of trafficking in persons, a special needs child with a disability (as defined in section 12102 of title 42), a child who has been a victim of physical or sexual abuse under circumstances that indicate that the child's health or welfare has been significantly harmed or threatened, or a child whose proposed sponsor clearly presents a risk of abuse, maltreatment, exploitation, or trafficking to the child based on all available objective evidence. The Secretary of Health and Human Services shall conduct follow-up services, during the pendency of removal proceedings, on children for whom a home study was conducted and is authorized to conduct follow-up services in cases involving children with mental health or other needs who could benefit from ongoing assistance from a social welfare agency. (C) Access to information Not later than 2 weeks after receiving a request from the Secretary of Health and Human Services, the Secretary of Homeland Security shall provide information necessary to conduct suitability assessments from appropriate Federal, State, and local law enforcement and immigration databases. Senate adds $300 million to ORR for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2028; this is a separate actor/account/date from DHS/ICE funds, not an actual expenditure, placement, screening finding or universal detention mandate. Funds may only support the five printed purpose categories. The background-check purpose shall include all seven items for their own named sponsor/household subjects; retain social security number or tax payer identification number as alternatives, in-person or virtual interview as alternatives, suitability study and all adult residents, and minimum fingerprint-based national criminal history/public-record/sex-offender checks. Do not turn this appropriation into a new universal sponsor citizenship or work-authorized-SSN condition. The child examination purpose has no printed age-12 floor, no CBP-encounter requirement, and covers tattoos or markings while the child is in ORR care; House 70116/70117 conditions are not imported. An examination purpose does not itself establish gang affiliation or danger, and the data-sharing child-labor/trafficking purposes do not establish actual exploitation findings. Potential sponsor expressly includes an individual or entity who applies for custody. The existing full 279 and 1232(c) authorities remain bound with category, placement, suitability, home-study and counsel/advocate protections; this funding is not first-ever placement vetting authority or an implicit repeal of child-protection rules. Exact background-check/use-of-funds conditions are represented as funding-purpose conditions, not a fabricated standalone universal placement deadline or verified practice. Specific protocol, actual placement and compliance/outcome application remain outside this literal candidate. Other H.R.1 component research and the 61 separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Senate 40001 asset line 2: (2) $2,283,000,000 is provided for procurement and acquisition of rotary-wing aircraft, equipment related to such aircraft and training simulators and program management for such aircraft, to provide for security of the maritime border; Senate 40001 asset line 3: (3) $266,000,000 is provided for procurement and acquisition of long-range unmanned aircraft and base stations, equipment related to such aircraft and base stations, and program management for such aircraft and base stations, to provide for security of the maritime border; Senate 40001 asset line 10: (10) $4,379,000,000 is provided for design, planning, engineering, recapitalization, construction, rebuilding, and improvement of, and program management for, shore facilities, of which-- (A) $425,000,000 is provided for design, planning, engineering, construction of, and program management for-- (i) the enlisted boot camp barracks and multi-use training center; (C) not more than $2,729,500,000 is provided for homeports and hangars for cutters and aircraft for which funds are appropriated under paragraph (1) through (9); and (D) $300,000,000 is provided for homeporting of the existing polar icebreaker commissioned into service in 2025; Senate 40001 asset line 11: (11) $2,200,000,000 is provided for aviation, cutter, and shore facility depot maintenance and maintenance of command, control, communication, computer, and cyber assets; Senate 40001 asset line 12: (12) $170,000,000 is provided for improving maritime domain awareness on the maritime border, at United States ports, at land-based facilities and in the cyber domain; and Senate 40001 asset line 13: (13) $75,000,000 is provided to contract the services of, acquire, or procure autonomous maritime systems.. Senate 40001 technical table amendment: (b) Technical and Conforming Amendment.--The analysis for chapter 11 of title 14, United States Code, is amended by adding at the end the following: subchapter v--coast guard mission readiness 1181. Special appropriations.. Senate separately prints maritime-border purposes in lines 1-3, operational maritime-border presence/security and interdiction of persons and controlled substances in lines 4-5, Arctic/Antarctic presence in 6-7, qualified-shipyard domestic icebreaking in 8, navigation/coastal security/inland search and rescue in 9, shore facilities in 10, depot and command/control/communication/computer/cyber maintenance in 11, multiple border/port/land/cyber domains in 12 and autonomous systems in 13. Whole original 1105/1131/1132/1133/1151/1156 acquisition/foreign-yard/UAS authorities are bound at exact extents; each bill override retains its own scope, not an exemption from all procurement, security, safety or other law. Selected exact Senate scholarship contributing-taxpayer scope and own-version boundaries follow. Senate own new 25F clause a: (a) Allowance of Credit.--In the case of an individual who is a citizen or resident of the United States (within the meaning of section 7701(a)(9)), there shall be allowed as a credit against the tax imposed by this chapter for the taxable year an amount equal to the aggregate amount of qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause b: (b) Limitations.-- (1) In general.--The credit allowed under subsection (a) to any taxpayer for any taxable year shall not exceed $1,700. (2) Reduction based on state credit.--The amount allowed as a credit under subsection (a) for a taxable year shall be reduced by the amount allowed as a credit on any State tax return of the taxpayer for qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause c: (c) Definitions.--For purposes of this section-- (1) Covered state.--The term `covered State' means one of the States, or the District of Columbia, that, for a calendar year, voluntarily elects to participate under this section and to identify scholarship granting organizations in the State, in accordance with subsection (g). (2) Eligible student.--The term `eligible student' means an individual who-- (A) is a member of a household with an income which, for the calendar year prior to the date of the application for a scholarship, is not greater than 300 percent of the area median gross income (as such term is used in section 42), and (B) is eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school. (3) Qualified contribution.--The term `qualified contribution' means a charitable contribution of cash to a scholarship granting organization that uses the contribution to fund scholarships for eligible students solely within the State in which the organization is listed pursuant to subsection (g). (4) Qualified elementary or secondary education expense.--The term `qualified elementary or secondary education expense' means any expense of an eligible student which is described in section 530(b)(3)(A). (5) Scholarship granting organization.--The term `scholarship granting organization' means any organization-- (A) which-- (i) is described in section 501(c)(3) and exempt from tax under section 501(a), and (ii) is not a private foundation, (B) which prevents the co-mingling of qualified contributions with other amounts by maintaining one or more separate accounts exclusively for qualified contributions, (C) which satisfies the requirements of subsection (d), and (D) which is included on the list submitted for the applicable covered State under subsection (g) for the applicable year. Senate own new 25F clause d: (d) Requirements for Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) In general.--An organization meets the requirements of this subsection if-- (A) such organization provides scholarships to 10 or more students who do not all attend the same school, (B) such organization spends not less than 90 percent of the income of the organization on scholarships for eligible students, (C) such organization does not provide scholarships for any expenses other than qualified elementary or secondary education expenses, (D) such organization provides a scholarship to eligible students with a priority for-- (i) students awarded a scholarship the previous school year, and (ii) after application of clause (i), any eligible students who have a sibling who was awarded a scholarship from such organization, (E) such organization does not earmark or set aside contributions for scholarships on behalf of any particular student, and (F) such organization-- (i) verifies the annual household income and family size of eligible students who apply for scholarships to ensure such students meet the requirement of subsection (c)(2)(A), and (ii) limits the awarding of scholarships to eligible students who are a member of a household for which the income does not exceed the amount established under subsection (c)(2)(A). (2) Prohibition on self-dealing.-- (A) In general.--A scholarship granting organization may not award a scholarship to any disqualified person. (B) Disqualified person.--For purposes of this paragraph, a disqualified person shall be determined pursuant to rules similar to the rules of section 4946. Senate own new 25F clause e: (e) Denial of Double Benefit.--Any qualified contribution for which a credit is allowed under this section shall not be taken into account as a charitable contribution for purposes of section 170. Senate own new 25F clause f: (f) Carryforward of Unused Credit.-- (1) In general.--If the credit allowable under subsection (a) for any taxable year exceeds the limitation imposed by section 26(a) for such taxable year reduced by the sum of the credits allowable under this subpart (other than this section, section 23, and section 25D), such excess shall be carried to the succeeding taxable year and added to the credit allowable under subsection (a) for such taxable year. (2) Limitation.--No credit may be carried forward under this subsection to any taxable year following the fifth taxable year after the taxable year in which the credit arose. For purposes of the preceding sentence, credits shall be treated as used on a first-in first-out basis. Senate own new 25F clause g: (g) State List of Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) List.-- (A) In general.--Not later than January 1 of each calendar year (or, with respect to the first calendar year for which this section applies, as early as practicable), a State that voluntarily elects to participate under this section shall provide to the Secretary a list of the scholarship granting organizations that meet the requirements described in subsection (c)(5) and are located in the State. (B) Process.--The election under this paragraph shall be made by the Governor of the State or by such other individual, agency, or entity as is designated under State law to make such elections on behalf of the State with respect to Federal tax benefits. (2) Certification.--Each list submitted under paragraph (1) shall include a certification that the individual, agency, or entity submitting such list on behalf of the State has the authority to perform this function. Senate own new 25F clause h: (h) Regulations and Guidance.--The Secretary shall issue such regulations or other guidance as the Secretary determines necessary to carry out the purposes of this section, including regulations or other guidance-- (1) providing for enforcement of the requirements under subsections (d) and (g), and (2) with respect to recordkeeping or information reporting for purposes of administering the requirements of this section.. Senate separate scholarship income exclusion: (b) Exclusion From Gross Income for Scholarships for Qualified Elementary or Secondary Education Expenses of Eligible Students.-- (1) In general.--Part III of subchapter B of chapter 1 is amended by inserting before section 140 the following new section: SEC. 139K. SCHOLARSHIPS FOR QUALIFIED ELEMENTARY OR SECONDARY EDUCATION EXPENSES OF ELIGIBLE STUDENTS. (a) In General.--In the case of an individual, gross income shall not include any amounts provided to such individual or any dependent of such individual pursuant to a scholarship for qualified elementary or secondary education expenses of an eligible student which is provided by a scholarship granting organization. (b) Definitions.--In this section, the terms `qualified elementary or secondary education expense', `eligible student', and `scholarship granting organization' have the same meaning given such terms under section 25F(c).. (2) Conforming amendment.--The table of sections for part III of subchapter B of chapter 1 is amended by inserting before the item relating to section 140 the following new item: Sec. 139K. Scholarships for qualified elementary or secondary education expenses of eligible students.. Senate own applicability dates: (c) Effective Date.-- (1) In general.--Except as otherwise provided in this subsection, the amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years ending after December 31, 2026. (2) Exclusion from gross income.--The amendments made by subsection (b) shall apply to amounts received after December 31, 2026, in taxable years ending after such date. Original printed geographic reference: (9) United States The term "United States" when used in a geographical sense includes only the States and the District of Columbia. Original education-expense reference and definitions: (3) Qualified elementary and secondary education expenses (A) In general The term "qualified elementary and secondary education expenses" means— (i) expenses for tuition, fees, academic tutoring, special needs services in the case of a special needs beneficiary, books, supplies, and other equipment which are incurred in connection with the enrollment or attendance of the designated beneficiary of the trust as an elementary or secondary school student at a public, private, or religious school, (ii) expenses for room and board, uniforms, transportation, and supplementary items and services (including extended day programs) which are required or provided by a public, private, or religious school in connection with such enrollment or attendance, and (iii) expenses for the purchase of any computer technology or equipment or Internet access and related services, if such technology, equipment, or services are to be used by the beneficiary and the beneficiary's family during any of the years the beneficiary is in school. Clause (iii) shall not include expenses for computer software designed for sports, games, or hobbies unless the software is predominantly educational in nature. (B) School The term "school" means any school which provides elementary education or secondary education (kindergarten through grade 12), as determined under State law. (C) Computer technology or equipment The term "computer technology or equipment" means computer software (as defined by section 197(e)(3)(B)), computer or peripheral equipment (as defined by section 168(i)(2)(B)), and fiber optic cable related to computer use. Senate 70411 new 25F(a) assigns citizen or resident of the United States (within the meaning of section 7701(a)(9)) to the contributing individual taxpayer who claims the contribution tax credit. This is a status-specific public-tax-benefit mechanism under the existing candidate issue boundary; it does not attach that phrase to the scholarship recipient or every student. Printed 7701(a)(9) defines United States when used in a geographical sense as only the States and District of Columbia; it is not silently rewritten as a printed 7701(b) citation or a categorical residence/territory/status eligibility outcome. Both own eligible-student definitions require household income at most 300 percent of area median gross income together with eligibility to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school; Senate expressly measures income for the calendar year prior to scholarship application. Neither printed eligible-student definition adds the Senate donor citizen/resident clause. This does not establish universal actual school enrollment, scholarship receipt or taxpayer eligibility. House credit limit is the greater of 10 percent of taxpayer adjusted gross income or $5,000, together with volume-cap allocation and State-credit reduction; Senate limit is $1,700 and its own State-credit reduction, voluntary covered-State/list mechanism and cash/within-State contribution requirements. They are not identical amounts, automatic credits for all residents, actual payments or a student immigration-status test. House 139J income exemption concerns amounts provided to any dependent of the individual and expressly denies subsection (a) to amounts received after December 31, 2029; Senate 139K concerns amounts provided to the individual or any dependent and does not print that House termination. Neither income clause imports the separate donor citizen/resident words or grants all students every benefit. House applies to taxable years ending after December 31, 2025 with its own received-after date for income exemption; Senate uses years ending after December 31, 2026 with its own received-after date. No tax-year-beginning formulation or House sunset copied into Senate. House complete 25F(g) retains $5 billion for each calendar year 2026 through 2029 and zero thereafter together with first-come allocation, State-share and high-use-year increase/nondecrease provisions; their future-year interaction is separately reserved as question 62 rather than silently resolved. Complete original geographic and education-expense definitions remain bound with their own qualifiers, not a new general citizenship/SSN/student gate. Exact donor mechanism is a source-grounded candidate; broader education/tax policy context is not automatically Immigration scope. No inferred motive, endorsement, new component stance, actual outcome or accepted individual tax/school application. Remaining cross-domain leads, full counterpart/package coverage and separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected House H.R. 1 provisions would fund border infrastructure and detention, set fiscal 2025 asylum filing/pending fee floors of $1,000/$100 and specified asylum/parole/TPS employment-authorization initial/renewal fee floors of $550, and limit those documents to at most six months. This is a whole-package passage choice, with qualifications.
